title: Phones and the internet: using them kindly and safely

summary.text: You type 'Fine' and press send. Your cousin reads it and feels hurt, though you were not angry at all, so what went wrong? In this lesson you find out how a phone carries a voice and a message across India in less than a second, and you test how much of a feeling is lost when a message has no face and no voice. Then you learn how to guard yourself and your devices against misuse, and why telling a trusted adult is the strongest thing you can do.
summary.art: A girl holding a phone showing the one word 'Fine', with a dotted line going over rooftops to a boy who reads the same word with a puzzled face.

intro.hook: Say 'Come here' in a happy voice. Now say it in an angry voice. Now write 'Come here' on a chit of paper. Which voice is on the paper?
intro.text: The paper holds the two words and nothing else. Your face and your voice stayed with you. A phone message is like that chit. A phone can carry your words to Kochi or Kohima in less than a second. Today you find out how the phone does that, what gets left behind on the way, and how to use phones and other devices kindly and safely.
intro.art: A chit of paper with 'Come here' written on it, and beside it two small faces of the same child, one smiling and one frowning.

outcomes: I can say how a phone sends a voice or a message to someone far away.
I can say what the internet is: many computers joined together by cables and radio waves.
I can explain why a typed message is easy to read in the wrong way, and what I can do about it.
I can name facts about me that are private, and say who I may share them with.
I can tell when a phone or another device is being misused, by me or by someone else.
I can say what to do when something on a screen feels wrong: stop, do not answer, keep it, and tell a trusted adult.
I can ask two questions before I believe or pass on something I see on a screen.
I can give one way a phone helps people and one way it can harm, and say why the same phone does both.

explanations.concept: A phone carries your voice and your words to someone far away
explanations.definition: A phone is a device that changes sound, words and pictures into a signal, sends the signal far away, and changes it back at the other end.
explanations.description: When you speak, your voice shakes the air. A tiny part inside the phone, called a microphone, feels the shaking. The phone changes the shaking into a signal. A signal is a pattern that can travel. The signal travels to the other phone. That phone changes the pattern back into shaking air, and your friend hears you. A typed message and a photo travel the same way, as patterns.
examples: A call from Chennai to Delhi covers about 1,800 kilometres. Your voice arrives in less than one second.
Shout from your balcony. Your real voice reaches about one street. A phone does not make your voice louder. The phone sends a pattern of your voice.
India has more than 100 crore mobile phone connections.

perspectives.who: Alexander Graham Bell, who received the first telephone patent in 1876
perspectives.explanation: Bell showed that a voice could travel along a wire as a changing electric current. He is usually named as the inventor of the telephone.

perspectives.who: Antonio Meucci, a poor Italian candle-maker in New York, and the inventor Elisha Gray
perspectives.explanation: Meucci built a working voice device years earlier and could not pay to keep his claim alive. Gray filed his own design on the same day as Bell. In 2002 the United States House of Representatives passed a resolution honouring Meucci's work. Historians still argue about who was first.

explanations.art: A girl speaking into a phone, wavy lines of sound going in, a row of dots and dashes travelling across a map of India, and wavy lines coming out of a second phone.
explanations.context: This card says what a phone does: it turns your voice and words into a pattern that can travel.

explanations.concept: A mobile phone talks to a tower with radio waves that we cannot see
explanations.definition: Radio waves are a kind of light that human eyes cannot see. A mobile phone sends and receives its signals as radio waves.
explanations.description: A mobile phone has no wire. So how does the signal leave the phone? The phone sends radio waves. Radio waves belong to the same family as the light from a torch. Our eyes cannot see them. They pass through air, glass and most walls. The waves reach the nearest mobile tower. From the tower, the signal goes on through cables to the tower nearest your friend.
examples: Walk into a lift or a basement and the call may break. Thick concrete and metal stop many of the radio waves.
A mobile tower in a city serves phones within about one or two kilometres of it. In open country one tower can reach much farther.
A radio, a television remote and Wi-Fi at home all use waves from this same family.

perspectives.who: Jagadish Chandra Bose, in Kolkata in 1895
perspectives.explanation: Bose sent very short radio waves across a hall and through walls. Reports of the time say the waves rang a bell and set off a little gunpowder in another room. He did not take out patents on this work, because he wanted everyone to be free to use it.

perspectives.who: Guglielmo Marconi, in 1901
perspectives.explanation: Marconi sent a radio signal across the Atlantic Ocean and built a business from it. Some historians have shown that the receiver he used was based on a design by Bose.

perspectives.who: Hedy Lamarr, a film actor, and George Antheil, a composer, in 1942
perspectives.explanation: They patented a way to make a radio signal hop quickly between channels so that nobody could block it. The idea was ignored for years. Ideas like theirs are used in Bluetooth and Wi-Fi today.

explanations.art: A phone in a child's hand with curved wave lines going out through a window to a tall tower, and a cable running from the foot of the tower into the ground.
explanations.context: This card explains how a phone with no wire still sends a signal: with radio waves, which are light we cannot see.

explanations.concept: The internet is millions of computers joined together, and many of the cables lie under the sea
explanations.definition: The internet is a network: a very large number of computers and phones joined so that any one can send a message to any other.
explanations.description: A network is many things joined together, like the lanes of a town. The internet is a network of computers. Most of the joining is done by cables. Inside the cables are threads of glass, as thin as a hair. Messages run along the glass as flashes of light. Cables as thick as a garden hose lie on the floor of the sea and join the countries. In India they come ashore at cities such as Mumbai, Chennai and Kochi.
examples: A video call from Madurai to an aunt in Singapore travels under the Bay of Bengal as flashes of light in glass.
Nearly all the messages that go between countries travel through undersea cables. Satellites carry only a small part.
When a ship's anchor cuts an undersea cable, the internet in whole countries can slow down until a repair ship mends it.

perspectives.who: Engineers who build networks
perspectives.explanation: The internet is a real, heavy thing: glass, metal, buildings and electricity. Words like 'the cloud' hide this. The photos you save are kept in large buildings full of computers, which need a lot of electricity and a lot of water for cooling.

perspectives.who: Tim Berners-Lee, who invented the World Wide Web in 1989
perspectives.explanation: The web is the pages and links that run on top of the internet. He gave it away free and has said it should belong to everyone. He has also said he is worried by how it is misused.

explanations.art: A cutaway of the sea with a cable lying on the sea floor between India and another coast, small flashes of light running inside it, and a fish swimming above.
explanations.context: This card says what the internet is made of, so the child knows it is a real thing and not magic.

explanations.concept: A message travels in small pieces and is put together again
explanations.definition: A packet is one small piece of a message, sent with the address of where it is going.
explanations.description: The internet does not send your photo in one lump. Your phone cuts the photo into many small pieces called packets. Each packet carries an address and a number. The packets may take different roads. At the other end, the phone puts them back in order by their numbers. If one packet is lost, the phone asks for that packet again.
examples: Tear a drawing into 8 numbered pieces. Send them across the room with different people. The person at the other end can still rebuild the drawing from the numbers.
When a video stops and shows a turning circle, the phone is waiting for packets that are late.
explanations.one_view: How packets work is a design that engineers chose and wrote down, so there is one account of it. Radia Perlman, an engineer, wrote a set of rules in 1985 that helps networks find a road with no loops, and it is still in use.
explanations.art: A photo of a mango cut into eight numbered squares, the squares flying along three different winding roads, and the whole mango photo rebuilt on a second phone.
explanations.context: This card shows that a message is cut into pieces and rebuilt, which is why the internet keeps working when one road is blocked.

explanations.concept: A phone is made from sand, rock and metals taken out of the Earth
explanations.definition: A phone is built from many materials, including glass made from sand and more than 30 different metals dug from the ground.
explanations.description: A phone looks smooth and clean. The glass began as sand. The wires hold copper. The battery holds metals called lithium and cobalt. People dig these out of the ground in mines. Most of the world's cobalt comes from one country in Africa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo. So a phone is a piece of the Earth, shaped by many hands. An old phone thrown in a bin wastes those metals and can poison soil and water.
examples: A phone holds a very small amount of gold, because gold carries electricity well and does not rust.
A shop that takes back old phones sends them to be taken apart, so the metals can be used again.
Using one phone for five years in place of two and a half means one phone fewer has to be dug out of the ground.

perspectives.who: Amnesty International, in a report of 2016
perspectives.explanation: The report found children working in small cobalt mines in the Congo, digging by hand for very little money. It asked phone and battery companies to check where their cobalt comes from.

perspectives.who: Repair workers in markets such as Ritchie Street in Chennai and Nehru Place in Delhi
perspectives.explanation: A phone that can be opened and mended lasts years longer. Many repairers say phones are now glued shut so that people buy a new one instead.

explanations.art: A phone opened like a book, with thin lines leading from its parts to a pile of sand, a copper rock, and a miner's hands holding a grey stone.
explanations.context: This card shows where a phone comes from, so that caring for a device and keeping it long makes sense.

explanations.concept: A sent message can be copied, so it cannot be fully taken back
explanations.definition: Once a message or a photo is sent, a copy exists on another device, and the sender no longer controls that copy.
explanations.description: Words you say aloud fade from the air. A sent message does not fade. A copy sits on your friend's phone. Your friend can show it, pass it on, or take a picture of the screen. Some apps let you delete a message. That removes one copy. It cannot remove a copy that someone has already saved. So the time to think is before you press send.
examples: You send a silly photo to one cousin. She forwards it to the family group of 40 people. Now 40 phones hold a copy.
A message deleted after ten minutes may already have been read and remembered.
A good habit: count to three and read the message once before you send it.
explanations.one_view: That a sent message can be copied is simply how devices work, and nobody disputes it.
explanations.art: One phone sending a photo, and the same photo appearing on more and more small phones spreading out like the branches of a tree.
explanations.context: This card explains why a message is different from spoken words: it stays, and it can multiply.

explanations.concept: A typed message leaves the face and the voice behind
explanations.definition: Tone is the feeling that a voice and a face add to words. A typed message carries the words without the tone.
explanations.description: When you talk, people read your face and hear your voice. That is how they know if you are joking. A typed message has only letters. So the reader has to guess your feeling, and often guesses wrongly. In 2005, a scientist named Justin Kruger and his team tested this. People who sent emails felt sure their tone would be understood about 78 times in 100. The readers got it right only about 56 times in 100. That is hardly better than tossing a coin.
examples: 'Okay.' can mean 'Yes, happily', 'I am upset' or 'I am busy'. The letters are the same each time.
A voice note or a call carries your voice, so less is lost.
A small picture face, called an emoji, puts back a little of the missing feeling. Even emojis are read differently by different people.

perspectives.who: Justin Kruger and Nicholas Epley, psychologists, in 2005
perspectives.explanation: The sender hears their own voice in their head while typing, so the message sounds clear to them. The reader does not get that voice. The sender forgets this.

perspectives.who: Letter writers and poets, for thousands of years
perspectives.explanation: Written words can carry deep feeling when the writer takes time and care. A hurried message is the problem, more than writing itself.

explanations.art: The word 'Okay.' in the middle, with three different faces around it: a smiling one, a sad one and a busy one.
explanations.context: This card explains why kind people still hurt each other by message: the reader cannot see the face or hear the voice.

explanations.concept: Unkind messages hurt a real person, and doing it again and again is bullying
explanations.definition: Bullying is hurting someone on purpose, again and again. When it is done with phones or the internet it is called cyberbullying.
explanations.description: There is always a person at the other end of a message. That person has a body, and feelings show up in the body. A cruel message can make a child's stomach hurt or keep them awake. On a phone the hurt can follow a child home, into their own room, at any hour. Misuse of a phone includes sending mean words, leaving one child out of a group on purpose, and passing on a photo to make people laugh at someone.
examples: Three children make a group and name it after a classmate's stammer. That is bullying, even if each child sent only one message.
A test before sending: would I say this to their face, with their grandparent standing beside them?
If you see bullying in a group, you can refuse to pass it on, say a kind word to the child, and tell a trusted adult.

perspectives.who: Naomi Eisenberger, a brain scientist, in 2003
perspectives.explanation: Her team left people out of a simple ball game on a screen. Parts of the brain that are busy during body pain also became busy when people were left out. She argues that being left out really hurts.

perspectives.who: Some people, who say 'they are only words on a screen'
perspectives.explanation: They hold that a child can switch the phone off and walk away. Children who have been bullied answer that the messages are still there when the phone is switched on again, and that everyone else has read them.

explanations.art: A child sitting on a bed at night looking at a glowing phone, with a small dark cloud over their stomach.
explanations.context: This card names one kind of misuse, bullying by message, and says why it hurts as much as bullying face to face.

explanations.concept: On a screen you cannot see who is really there
explanations.definition: Anyone can type any name and use any picture. A person on a screen may not be who they say they are.
explanations.description: At your door you can see who has come. On a screen you see only a name and a picture, and both can be false. Some people use this to trick others. A caller may say 'I am from the bank' to get money. A stranger in a game may say 'I am eight, like you' and may be a grown-up. A message may say 'You have won a prize, press here'. A safe rule is this. If you have not met the person in real life with your family, they are a stranger.
examples: A bank sends a secret number to a phone, called a one-time password or OTP. A real bank never asks you to read it out. Anyone who asks for it is trying to steal.
A message with a link from a number you do not know: do not press it. Show a grown-up.
A stranger who says 'Keep this our secret' is giving you the clearest sign to tell an adult.
explanations.one_view: That names and pictures on a screen can be false is a plain fact about how accounts work. People disagree only about how to guard against it.
explanations.art: A friendly cartoon child's picture on a phone screen, and behind the phone a shadow of a much taller figure holding it.
explanations.context: This card teaches the most important fact for safety: a name on a screen proves nothing about who is typing.

explanations.concept: Some facts about you are private, and passwords are never shared with friends
explanations.definition: Private information is anything that lets a stranger find you, pretend to be you, or get into your family's accounts.
explanations.description: Some facts are like the key to your house. Your full name, your home address, your school's name, your phone number and your photo can lead a stranger to you. A password is a secret word that opens an account. An account is your own space in an app. A password is shared only with your parent or the adult who looks after you. A best friend today may not be a best friend next month, and the password will still work.
examples: A photo in your school uniform, standing at your gate, tells a stranger your school and your house in one picture.
A game asks for your birthday and address to 'unlock a prize'. Ask a grown-up first. Most games do not need these.
A strong password is long. Three odd words in a row, such as 'idli-kite-monsoon', are hard to guess and easy to remember.

perspectives.who: People who study privacy, such as the legal scholar Usha Ramanathan in India
perspectives.explanation: They argue that small facts about a person add up. One fact seems harmless. Many facts together can show where a person lives, what they buy and who they meet.

perspectives.who: Many companies that run free apps
perspectives.explanation: They say that collecting facts about users lets them keep the app free and show each person what they like. Critics answer that the user is paying with their private life.

explanations.art: A house key drawn large, with small pictures hanging from its ring: a school badge, a door number, a phone number and a padlock.
explanations.context: This card says which facts to guard and why a password is different from an ordinary secret.

explanations.concept: Ask before you take or share someone's picture
explanations.definition: Consent means a person freely says yes. A photo or video of someone should be taken and shared only with their consent.
explanations.description: A photo of you is a piece of you that travels without you. So each person decides about their own picture. Before you take a photo of a friend, ask. Before you send that photo to anyone, ask again. If they say no, or say nothing, the answer is no. The same holds for you. You may say 'Please do not post that' to a friend, a relative or a teacher.
examples: Your little brother is crying with rasam on his shirt. A video would be funny today. Ask yourself how he will feel when his class sees it in five years.
Taking a photo of someone who is changing clothes or bathing is never all right. Tell a trusted adult if anyone does this or asks for this.

perspectives.who: Parents and grandparents who share children's photos in family WhatsApp groups, a common habit in Indian families
perspectives.explanation: They share children's photos out of love, so that relatives far away can watch the children grow.

perspectives.who: Children's rights groups, and the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child in a statement of 2021
perspectives.explanation: They hold that children have a right to privacy online, and that adults should think about the child's own wishes before posting.

explanations.art: A girl holding up a phone camera and asking with a raised hand, and her friend answering with a thumbs up.
explanations.context: This card gives the rule for cameras: every person decides about their own picture.

explanations.concept: Not everything on a screen is true
explanations.definition: A rumour is a story passed from person to person that nobody has checked.
explanations.description: Anyone can type anything and send it to thousands of people. A false story often travels faster than a true one, because it is surprising. In 2018, the scientist Soroush Vosoughi and his team studied about 126,000 stories on one large social site. False stories reached people about six times faster than true ones. So before you believe or forward something, ask two questions. Who is saying this? How do they know?
examples: A forwarded message says 'School is closed tomorrow because of rain'. The check is to ask the school or a teacher, not to forward the message.
A picture can be changed, and computer programs can now make pictures and voices of things that never happened.
A message that says 'Send this to ten people quickly' is asking you to skip the checking.

perspectives.who: Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy and Sinan Aral, in the journal Science, 2018
perspectives.explanation: They found that people, more than automatic programs, spread false stories, mostly because false stories felt new and surprising.

perspectives.who: The Nyaya school of Indian philosophy, in the Nyaya Sutras of Gautama, sutras 1.1.3 to 1.1.7
perspectives.explanation: Nyaya lists four ways of knowing: seeing for yourself, reasoning, comparing, and the word of a trustworthy person. A word counts only if the speaker truly knows the thing and wishes to tell it honestly.

explanations.art: A phone showing a message with many forward arrows, and a child holding a magnifying glass over it with two question marks.
explanations.context: This card gives two questions to ask before believing or passing on anything seen on a screen.

explanations.concept: Many apps and games are built to keep you looking
explanations.definition: Some features of apps, such as the next video starting by itself, are designed so that people find it hard to stop.
explanations.description: Have you ever meant to watch one video and watched six? That is partly by design. In many apps the next video starts without being asked. The page never reaches a bottom. A red dot or a ping calls you back. Many free apps earn money from advertisements, so more minutes of looking means more money. Knowing this helps. When you feel the tug to keep going, the tug was built on purpose, and you can still choose.
examples: Turn off 'play next video automatically' with a grown-up, and see if stopping becomes easier.
A game that gives a prize 'only if you come back tomorrow' is using the same trick.
Decide before you start: 'two videos', or 'until the timer rings at 20 minutes'.

perspectives.who: Aza Raskin, the designer who invented the page that scrolls without end, in 2006
perspectives.explanation: He has said he is sorry he made it. He meant to save people effort and did not foresee how much time it would take from them.

perspectives.who: The makers of apps and games, in their public statements about parental controls
perspectives.explanation: They say they give people what people enjoy, and that parents can set time limits in the settings.

perspectives.who: Tristan Harris, who once worked on design at Google
perspectives.explanation: He argues that when thousands of engineers work to hold a child's attention, it is not a fair contest, and that the designs should change.

explanations.art: A child's thumb on a phone, with a long strip of video pictures running off the bottom of the screen and curling away with no end.
explanations.context: This card explains why stopping is hard, so that the child does not blame themselves and can plan ahead.

explanations.concept: A screen held close for a long time tires the eyes and can push sleep later
explanations.definition: Looking at something near for a long time makes the small muscles of the eye work without rest. Bright light late in the evening tells the body it is still day.
explanations.description: To look at something near, small muscles inside your eyes squeeze. Held for an hour, they get tired, and you blink less, so your eyes feel dry. Eye doctors suggest the 20-20-20 habit. Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away, which is about 6 metres, for 20 seconds. Bright screens late at night also matter. Your body reads bright light as daytime and holds back its sleep signal.
examples: Look out of the window at the farthest tree or tower you can see. That rests the eye muscles.
In a study of 2015, the scientist Anne-Marie Chang found that adults who read on a bright screen before bed took about 10 minutes longer to fall asleep than when they read a paper book.
Keep the phone at arm's length, and out of the bedroom at night.

perspectives.who: The Indian Academy of Pediatrics, the children's doctors of India, in guidelines of 2021
perspectives.explanation: They advise less than 2 hours of screen time a day for children of 5 to 10 years, with play outdoors, sleep and family time coming first.

perspectives.who: Eye researchers such as Pei-Chang Wu in Taiwan
perspectives.explanation: They find that time outdoors in daylight protects children's eyes from becoming short-sighted, and that the missing daylight may matter more than the screen itself.

explanations.art: A child looking up from a tablet to a far-off coconut tree through a window, with a small clock showing 20 minutes.
explanations.context: This card says what long screen use does to the body, and gives one simple habit to rest the eyes.

explanations.concept: Is screen time bad for children? Scientists disagree
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that sleep, play and time with people matter for children. They disagree about how much harm screens themselves do.
explanations.description: You may have heard that screens are bad for children. The evidence is mixed. Some scientists find that children who use screens a lot are a little less happy. Others look at the same numbers and find the link is very small. It is also hard to know which comes first. Does the phone make a child sad, or does a sad child pick up the phone more? What a child does on the screen matters too. A video call with a grandparent is not the same as two hours of videos alone.
examples: One hour spent drawing on a tablet with a cousin, and one hour scrolling alone, both count as 'one hour of screen time'.
In November 2024, Australia passed a law that keeps children under 16 off social media apps. Other countries are watching to see what happens.

perspectives.who: Jean Twenge, a psychologist, in her book 'iGen' of 2017, and Jonathan Haidt in 'The Anxious Generation' of 2024
perspectives.explanation: They point out that sadness and worry among teenagers rose in several countries after about 2012, when smartphones became common. They argue that phones are a main cause.

perspectives.who: Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski, in a study of 2019
perspectives.explanation: They studied records of more than 3 lakh young people. Screen use explained less than half of one part in a hundred of the differences in how happy the young people were. They wrote that eating potatoes had about as strong a link.

perspectives.who: Candice Odgers, a psychologist who studies children's lives
perspectives.explanation: She argues that blaming phones may hide other causes of unhappiness, such as poverty, loneliness and violence, and that for some lonely children the phone is where they find friends.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a phone on one side and a ball, a pillow and a group of friends on the other, with a question mark above.
explanations.context: This card is honest that scientists have not settled how much screens harm children, and gives the best case on each side.

explanations.concept: When something feels wrong: stop, do not answer, keep it, and tell a trusted adult
explanations.definition: A trusted adult is a grown-up you know well who keeps you safe and listens to you, such as a parent, a grandparent, an older relative or a teacher.
explanations.description: Your body often knows first. Your stomach tightens, or your face goes hot. If a message, a picture, a call or a person on a screen makes you feel scared, confused or dirty, do four things. Stop. Do not answer. Do not delete it, because the adult needs to see it. Tell a trusted adult the same day. It is never your fault, even if you pressed something you were told not to press. If the first adult does not listen, tell another.
examples: Childline, on the number 1098, is a free phone service in India for any child who needs help. The emergency number 112 reaches the police, an ambulance or the fire service.
For money tricks on the phone, families in India can call the cyber helpline 1930.
Words you can use: 'Something on the phone scared me. Please look at it with me.'

perspectives.who: Children, when researchers ask why they did not tell anyone
perspectives.explanation: Many say they were afraid the phone would be taken away, or that they would be scolded. So the telling stops.

perspectives.who: Child-safety workers
perspectives.explanation: They ask parents to make one promise in advance: 'If you tell me, I will not be angry and I will not punish you for telling.' Children who have heard that promise tell sooner.

explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a raised hand for stop, a closed mouth, a phone with a small lock on the message, and a child showing the phone to a grown-up who is kneeling down to listen.
explanations.context: This card gives the four steps to take when anything on a device feels wrong, and says who a trusted adult is.

explanations.concept: Guard the device: a lock, an ask-first rule, and the same care for tablets, computers, televisions and speakers
explanations.definition: Misuse of a device means using it to harm, to trick, to spy or to take what is not yours, or using someone's device without their leave.
explanations.description: A phone holds a family's photos, messages and money. So it needs a guard, like a front door. A screen lock is a secret number or pattern that opens the phone. Ask before you use anyone's device. Ask before you download an app, press a link or buy anything in a game. Tablets, computers, smart televisions and talking speakers are joined to the internet too. They can have cameras and microphones. The same rules guard all of them.
examples: A found phone or a pen drive on the road is not yours to open. Give it to a grown-up.
A game says 'Buy 500 coins'. That is real money from a real bank account.
A device is also a thing that can be damaged. Keep it dry, do not charge it under a pillow where it can get hot, and never touch a charger with wet hands.
Looking through another person's messages without asking is misuse, even at home.
explanations.one_view: These are agreed safety habits. The disagreements about how much freedom a child should have with devices are given in the card on screen time.
explanations.art: A phone, a tablet, a laptop, a television and a round speaker in a row, each with a small padlock and a small 'ask first' hand.
explanations.context: This card lists the habits that guard a device from misuse, and shows they apply to every device that joins the internet.

explanations.concept: A phone used well saves lives and joins people, and not everyone has one
explanations.definition: A tool is neither good nor bad. What it does depends on how it is used and who gets to use it.
explanations.description: The same phone that can carry a cruel message can call an ambulance. Phones bring weather warnings to fishing boats. They let a child in Bengaluru see a grandparent in Shillong. They read text aloud for people who cannot see. A study on the Kerala coast shows how much they can change. Yet not every family has a phone. In India, far fewer women than men own a smartphone, so many women and girls are left out of what phones can do.
examples: Between 1997 and 2001, mobile towers came to the Kerala coast. The economist Robert Jensen found that fishers began to phone the markets from their boats to find where fish were needed. Fish that used to be thrown away unsold were no longer wasted, and prices became fairer.
In an emergency a child can dial 112 from any phone, even one that is locked.
A person who cannot hear can talk with friends by video in sign language.

perspectives.who: The GSMA, a worldwide group of mobile companies, in yearly reports on women and phones
perspectives.explanation: The reports find that in many countries women are less likely than men to own a phone, often because of cost and because families do not allow it.

perspectives.who: Some village councils and families in India
perspectives.explanation: They have stopped girls from having phones, saying it keeps them safe. Many girls and women's groups answer that this takes away their schooling, their work and their way to call for help.

explanations.art: A small fishing boat on the sea off Kerala with a woman on the shore at a fish market, each holding a phone, joined by a dotted line.
explanations.context: This card balances the warnings: the same device does great good, and being left without one is also a harm.

explanations.concept: People are not the only beings who send messages far
explanations.definition: Many living beings send signals over long distances, using sound, smell, touch and movement.
explanations.description: Long before phones, other beings were sending messages across forests and fields. Elephants make rumbles so deep that human ears cannot hear them. These rumbles carry for several kilometres. A honey bee who finds flowers comes home and dances, and her sisters read from the dance which way to fly and how far. The phone is one more way of sending a message, among very many on Earth.
examples: A male koel calls from a mango tree in March, and a koel far across the neighbourhood answers.
Ants leave a line of smell on the ground. The ants who follow read the smell as 'food this way'.

perspectives.who: Katy Payne, who studied elephants in the 1980s
perspectives.explanation: She felt a throbbing in the air near elephants in a zoo, recorded it, and showed that elephants call to each other with sounds below human hearing.

perspectives.who: Karl von Frisch, who studied honey bees and shared a Nobel Prize in 1973
perspectives.explanation: He worked out the meaning of the bees' dance. Some scientists of his time doubted that an insect could do this, and later tests with radar tracking supported him.

explanations.art: An elephant herd on one side of a forest and another herd far away, joined by long low wavy lines along the ground, with a honey bee dancing on a comb in a corner.
explanations.context: This card places the phone among the many ways living beings send messages, so the child does not think messaging began with people.

explanations.concept: Some voices on a phone are computer programs. Do they understand?
explanations.definition: A chatbot or a voice assistant is a computer program that answers in words. Scientists and philosophers disagree about whether such a program understands anything.
explanations.description: Some voices that answer you are not people. A voice assistant and a chatbot are computer programs. They have learnt patterns from a huge amount of human writing. They can be helpful, and they can also be wrong while sounding sure. A program cannot come to your house to help you, so it is not your trusted adult. Does the program understand what it says? Science has no agreed test for understanding, and no final definition of it. So this question is open.
examples: In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum wrote a simple program named ELIZA that turned a person's sentences into questions. Many people who typed to ELIZA felt truly listened to, and this alarmed him.
Ask a chatbot and a grandparent the same question about your own town. Notice who can say how they know.

perspectives.who: Alan Turing, a mathematician, in 1950
perspectives.explanation: He proposed a test. If you chat by typing and cannot tell the machine from a person, he said, it is fair to say the machine thinks.

perspectives.who: John Searle, a philosopher, in 1980
perspectives.explanation: He imagined a man in a room who follows a rule book to answer Chinese letters without knowing any Chinese. The answers are perfect, and the man understands nothing. Searle argued that a program is like that man.

perspectives.who: Thinkers of Advaita Vedanta in India, and some modern scientists who hold a view called panpsychism
perspectives.explanation: They hold that consciousness is the ground of everything that exists. On this view the question changes. It asks what form awareness takes in a machine, and nobody knows the answer.

explanations.art: A phone with a speech bubble coming out of it and no face behind the bubble, and a child tilting her head, wondering.
explanations.context: This card says that some answers on a device come from programs, that they can be wrong, and that nobody yet knows if a program understands.

explanations.concept: Old tests for words: is it true, is it kind, is it useful, is this the right time?
explanations.definition: Teachers in ancient India set out tests a person can put to their words before speaking. The same tests work for a message.
explanations.description: People worried about hurtful words long before phones. About 2,500 years ago the Buddha gave five tests for speech. Is it said at the right time? Is it true? Is it gentle? Is it useful? Is it said with goodwill? In the Tamil book Tirukkural, the poet Tiruvalluvar wrote that using harsh words when sweet ones are at hand is like eating unripe fruit when ripe fruit is there. These are teachings and not science. You can still test them yourself.
examples: Before sending 'You were so slow in the race', try the tests. It may be true. Is it gentle? Is it useful? Is this the right time?
A true thing can be said kindly: 'I waited for you at the finish line.'

perspectives.who: The Buddha, in the Vaca Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 5.198
perspectives.explanation: Speech is well spoken when it is timely, true, gentle, beneficial and spoken with a mind of goodwill.

perspectives.who: Tiruvalluvar, in the Tirukkural, chapter 10 on sweet speech, kural 100
perspectives.explanation: To speak harshly when kind words are available is like choosing the unripe fruit and leaving the ripe one.

perspectives.who: People who value plain speaking, in many cultures
perspectives.explanation: They warn that 'be kind' can be used to silence someone who must say a hard truth, such as a child who needs to report a wrong. A hard truth told to a trusted adult passes every test that matters.

explanations.art: A message bubble passing through four small gates in a row, labelled true, kind, useful and right time, before reaching a send button.
explanations.context: This card brings old Indian teachings about speech to the new question of what to send.

agreed.text: Children who spend more time outdoors in daylight are less likely to become short-sighted.
agreed.evidence: In a trial led by the eye doctor Pei-Chang Wu in Taiwan, reported in 2018, about 700 Class 1 children were followed for a year. Schools in one group sent children outdoors for more hours each week. Fewer children in that group became short-sighted, and their eyes changed more slowly.

agreed.text: Radio waves were predicted with mathematics before anyone had made or detected one.
agreed.evidence: James Clerk Maxwell published equations in 1865 that said such waves must exist and must travel at the speed of light. Heinrich Hertz made and detected them in his laboratory in 1887 and 1888, and their speed matched.

agreed.text: Old phones and other electronic waste hold valuable metals and also poisons, and most of the world's electronic waste is not yet collected properly.
agreed.evidence: The United Nations Global E-waste Monitor of 2024 counted about 62 billion kilograms of electronic waste made in 2022, and found that less than a quarter was recorded as collected and recycled properly.

challenging.claim: Mobile towers made the house sparrows disappear from Indian cities.
challenging.who: Many city residents and some bird-watchers in India, from about 2005 onwards
challenging.for: Sparrows became rare in many city centres in the same years that towers multiplied. A few field studies in Europe, such as one by Alfonso Balmori in Spain in 2007, found fewer sparrows where radio signals were stronger.
challenging.against: Those studies could not separate towers from other changes in the same places. Sparrows lost their nesting holes when tiled roofs gave way to concrete and glass, and their chicks lost insect food to pesticides and paved ground. Sparrows still thrive in many towns that are full of towers. A committee of the Environment Ministry in 2011 asked for more study and did not find the claim proven.
challenging.context: A popular belief about phones and other beings. Most bird scientists think loss of nest sites and insects is the main cause, and the question is not fully closed.

challenging.claim: The radio waves from mobile phones cause cancer.
challenging.who: Some doctors and campaigners. In 2011 the cancer research agency of the World Health Organization placed these waves in its group 'possibly' causing cancer
challenging.for: A few studies of very heavy phone users found slightly more of one kind of brain tumour. The agency judged the evidence too weak to prove harm and too uncertain to rule it out.
challenging.against: Radio waves from phones carry far too little energy to break the molecules in cells, which is how X-rays do harm. Brain cancer has not become more common in countries where nearly everyone now uses a phone.
challenging.context: A fear many families have heard. Most scientists judge the risk to be very small or absent, and studies continue.

challenging.claim: Children should not have a smartphone or social media until they are 14 or 16.
challenging.who: The psychologist Jonathan Haidt and parent groups in several countries. Australia made a law for under-16s in 2024
challenging.for: Childhood needs free play, sleep and face-to-face friendship, and apps are designed to hold attention. A shared rule also frees each child from being the only one left out.
challenging.against: Researchers such as Candice Odgers say the evidence of harm is weak, that bans are hard to enforce, and that they cut off children who find help and friends online. Others say teaching safe use early works better than a wall.
challenging.context: A live argument among scientists, parents and governments. It is here so the family can talk about their own rule and the reasons for it.

challenging.claim: Writing and screens weaken memory and thinking, because people stop holding things in their own minds.
challenging.who: Socrates, in Plato's dialogue Phaedrus (sections 274 to 275), said this of writing about 2,400 years ago. Some teachers say it of phones today
challenging.for: A study by Betsy Sparrow in 2011 found that people remember a fact less well when they expect to be able to look it up later.
challenging.against: In the same study people remembered better where to find the fact. Writing, printing and libraries were each feared in their time, and each let people think about more than one memory can hold.
challenging.context: A very old worry about every new way of keeping words. It shows the question about phones is part of a long argument.

big_questions.q: You typed 'Fine' and meant it kindly. Your cousin read 'Fine' and felt hurt. Where was the meaning of the message: in you, in the letters, or in your cousin?
big_questions.hint: Think about what actually travelled through the phone, and what each of you added to it.

big_questions.q: A friend on a video call is 2,000 kilometres away and you can see her smile. A neighbour is behind a wall and you cannot see him. Which of them is nearer to you?
big_questions.hint: Try measuring 'near' in more than one way: with a tape, with your eyes, with how quickly they could help you.

big_questions.q: If you would never say a thing to someone's face, why does it feel easier to type it?
big_questions.hint: Notice what your own body does when you see a face change in front of you, and what it does when there is only a screen.

big_questions.q: The same phone can call an ambulance and can carry a cruel message. Is a phone good, bad, or neither?
big_questions.hint: Try the same question on a knife, a matchstick and a word. See if your answer stays the same.

big_questions.q: A chatbot gives a kind and correct answer. A person gives a kind and correct answer. Is there any difference between the two answers?
big_questions.hint: Ask what you could check from outside, and what you could never check from outside, even for a person.

big_questions.q: A photo of you is on forty phones. Who does the photo belong to now?
big_questions.hint: Think about who took it, who is in it, who holds a copy, and who gets hurt if it is misused.

big_questions.q: How do you know that anything you were told today is true, if you did not see it yourself?
big_questions.hint: List three things you believe that you have never seen. For each, ask who told you and how they knew.

big_questions.q: An elephant's rumble and a phone call both carry a message across kilometres. Is a phone part of nature?
big_questions.hint: Trace what a phone is made from and who made it. Then ask where nature stops.

big_questions.q: Is keeping a secret always wrong, always right, or does it depend? How would you tell a safe secret from an unsafe one?
big_questions.hint: Compare a surprise birthday gift with a secret a stranger asks you to keep. Notice who the secret protects.

story.title: The Word That Cost Nothing
story.note: A made-up story set in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. Meenakshi, Arul and Saroja athai are imagined. What is real: India's public telegram service ran for more than 160 years and closed in July 2013. Telegrams were charged by the word, so people chose each word with care. The price in the story is imagined.
text: Meenakshi was seven, and she had her mother's phone for ten minutes. On the screen was a video from Sports Day. Her cousin Arul, who was eight and lived in Kochi, was running the fifty-metre race. He came last. In the video he was laughing as he crossed the line, and so was everyone else.
Meenakshi laughed too. She typed with one finger: 'You are so slow.' She pressed send. Then she went to find the murukku tin.

When she came back there was no answer. There was no answer after lunch. In the evening her mother's phone rang, and it was Arul's mother. 'He has not come out of his room,' she said. 'Somebody told him he is slow.'
Meenakshi's stomach went tight. 'But I was laughing when I wrote it,' she said. 'He was laughing in the video!'
On the swing in the corner sat Saroja athai, her grandfather's sister, who was eighty-one. For thirty years she had worked at the telegraph office in Thanjavur. She put down her tumbler of coffee.
'Show me what you sent,' she said. Meenakshi showed her. Saroja athai read the four words slowly. 'I see the words,' she said. 'I do not see any laughing. Where did you put the laughing?'
Meenakshi looked at the screen. The words sat there, small and grey. 'It was in my face,' she said at last.
'Then it is still in your face,' said Saroja athai. 'It did not go to Kochi.'
Meenakshi pressed on the message and chose delete. The words vanished. 'There. It is gone.'
'From your phone,' said Saroja athai. 'Has it gone from Arul?'
Meenakshi said nothing.

'When I was a young woman,' said Saroja athai, 'people came to my counter to send telegrams. A telegram was a message sent along a wire, tapped out in short and long beeps. I tapped them myself. Every word cost money. So a man would stand at my counter for ten minutes, cutting his message down. He would write: Father ill come soon. Four words. He had weighed each one in his hand like a coin.'
'Did people send unkind telegrams?' asked Meenakshi.
'Hardly ever. Nobody pays to be rude.' Saroja athai smiled. 'Your message cost nothing. So you did not weigh it. That is the only difference between you and that man. He was not kinder than you.'
Meenakshi's brother Karthik, who was five, had been listening from the floor. 'But it did cost something,' he said. 'Arul is crying.'
Nobody spoke for a moment. The swing creaked.
'So who paid?' asked Saroja athai quietly.

Meenakshi thought about that. In the old days the sender paid, at the counter, before the words left. Now the words left free. And the one who read them paid afterwards, in his stomach, in his room in Kochi.
'Can I call him?' she asked her mother. 'Not type. Call. With the video on.'
Arul's face came up on the screen. His eyes were red. For a second Meenakshi could not say anything, because now she could see him, and seeing him made her own eyes sting.
'I was laughing when I wrote it,' she said. 'Like you were laughing in the race. The laughing did not come through. I am sorry.'

Arul sniffed. He looked at her face for a long moment, the way you look at the sky to see if the rain is over. 'You are slow too,' he said. 'You took the whole day to call.' And then he grinned, and she could see the grin, and that settled it.
After the call, Meenakshi sat beside Saroja athai on the swing. 'Athai, the phone is faster than your telegraph. It can send a photo. It can send a whole film.'
'It can,' said Saroja athai.
'Then why could it not send one laugh?'
'It sent the laugh just now,' said Saroja athai, 'when you let it carry your face. The machine carries what you give it. This morning you gave it four words and kept the rest.'

Meenakshi pushed the swing with her toe. Somewhere under the sea, she knew, flashes of light were carrying other people's words to other people's cousins. She wondered how many of those words had been weighed.
story.epiphany: A message costs the sender nothing, so the sender does not weigh it. The cost is still there. It is paid later, by the one who reads it.
ask: Meenakshi deleted the message. What was gone, and what was not gone?
Saroja athai said people rarely sent unkind telegrams. Do you think people were kinder then, or was something else different?
Is there a way to 'weigh' a message when sending it costs nothing?
Arul believed Meenakshi when he saw her face. What did her face tell him that her words could not?

how_we_found_out.story: For most of history, people held that a message could go only as far and as fast as someone could carry it. A runner, a horse or a ship took the letter. This fitted everything people saw: words do not move by themselves. In the 1830s and 1840s the electric telegraph showed that a pattern of beeps could run along a wire far faster than any horse. India's first telegraph line was tried near Kolkata in 1850. In 1876 the telephone sent a voice along a wire. Still, people held that a wire was needed. In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell worked out with mathematics that invisible waves should be able to cross empty space. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made such waves. In 1895, in Kolkata, Jagadish Chandra Bose sent them through walls. In 1901 Guglielmo Marconi sent a signal across an ocean. On 29 October 1969 two computers in California were joined, and the first message between them was 'LO', because the system crashed before the word 'LOGIN' was finished. That link grew into the internet. On 3 April 1973 the engineer Martin Cooper made the first call from a hand-held mobile phone. India's first mobile call was made on 31 July 1995.
how_we_found_out.who: James Clerk Maxwell, Heinrich Hertz, Jagadish Chandra Bose, Guglielmo Marconi, Hedy Lamarr, Martin Cooper, Radia Perlman, Tim Berners-Lee
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A message can travel only if a person or a wire carries it. This was believable because nobody could see or feel radio waves, and every message anyone had ever sent had needed a carrier.

roots.context: You have tested how much of a feeling is lost when a message has no face. Now we ask what a message is, and what that tells us about ourselves and other people.

deep_truth.truth: You wrote one word on a chit, and your family guessed your feeling from it. They guessed wrongly about half the time. When they heard your voice, they guessed right far more often. The word on the chit never changed. So the meaning was not inside the word, and each reader finished the message in their own body.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'I sent my message' as if the meaning travelled whole, like a parcel. That way of speaking puts all of the message on the sender's side and makes the reader only a receiver. The test shows the reader builds half of it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the message without a face test, the same written word was read as happy by one person and as upset by another, and the number of right guesses rose when the voice was added and rose again when the face was added.

three.who_am_i: You found that your feeling does not leave your body with your words. The other person has to grow it again in their own body. So you are not sealed off from others. A part of what you mean lives in whoever is listening to you.
three.what_is_life: Elephants rumble, bees dance and ants lay trails of smell. Living beings keep reaching towards one another with signals. A being with no way to send or receive would be alone in a way no living being ever is.
three.what_is_this_world: Your voice becomes shaking air, then a pattern, then radio waves, then flashes of light in glass, then a feeling in a cousin far away. The world lets one pattern pass through all these forms. The phone, the sea cable and your cousin's ear are parts of one path.

roots.thread: A phone seems to join two separate people with a line. The test suggests something closer. A message is not finished when it leaves you, and it is not finished until someone reads it. So one message is made by two people together. The same is true of every word spoken across a room. Consciousness is the ground that both people arise from, which is why one can grow the other's feeling at all. Many scientists do not take this last step, and their view is given below.

teachings.teaching: Words that cause no distress, that are true, pleasant and helpful, are called the discipline of speech.
teachings.link: The verse treats speaking as something you practise, like a sport. The lesson's test shows why practice is needed: the sender cannot feel how the words will land without stopping to imagine the reader.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net, as explained by the Chinese Buddhist teacher Fazang in the 7th century CE
teachings.teaching: Imagine a net that stretches without end, with a shining jewel at every knot. Each jewel reflects every other jewel.
teachings.link: The internet is a real net with a device at each knot, and each device can show what any other sends. The old image goes further than the cables do. It says each thing holds the others, and not only that they are joined.

teachings.teaching: A burn from fire heals inside. A wound burnt in by the tongue does not heal.
teachings.link: This meets the card about copies. A typed word stays on forty phones long after the sender has forgotten it.

science.text: When people watch another person's face show a feeling, some of the same parts of their own brain and body become active as when they feel it themselves. Scientists link this to how we understand each other.

Radio waves and the flashes of light in glass fibre are one kind of thing. They are electromagnetic waves, which are invisible ripples that travel through air, glass and even empty space. They differ only in length. Visible light is the same kind of wave.

other_view.who: Claude Shannon, the engineer who founded the mathematics of communication in 1948, and many scientists after him
other_view.view: Shannon wrote that the meaning of a message has nothing to do with the engineering problem. On this view a message is a pattern that is copied from one place to another, and feelings are separate events in two separate brains. Nothing is shared except the pattern.

practice.title: One breath before send
practice.say: Sit with your child and hold a phone that is switched off. Say: 'Think of someone you might send a message to. Close your eyes and see their face.' Wait. 'Now take one slow breath in, and one slow breath out. Imagine them reading your message. What does their face do?' Wait. 'That breath is your send button. Whenever you are about to send, take it first.' Do it three times, with three different people in mind.
practice.kid: Hold the phone without switching it on. Close your eyes. See the face of someone you might write to. Breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly. Picture their face as they read your words. Do this three times, for three different people.

ask: When your family read your chit wrongly, whose mistake was it: yours, theirs, or nobody's?
If half of a message is made by the reader, can you ever be fully understood by anyone?
A bee reads her sister's dance and flies to the right flowers. Is that the same kind of understanding as reading a message?
roots.art: Two children far apart, each with a hand on their own chest, and a single thread of light running between them through a phone, a tower and a cable under the sea.

open_questions.q: Do screens change how a child's attention grows?
open_questions.why_open: Children who use screens a lot differ from other children in many ways, such as sleep, family income and how much adults talk with them. Scientists cannot fairly make some children use screens for years and others not, so they cannot yet separate the screen from the rest.

open_questions.q: Does a computer program that answers in sentences understand anything?
open_questions.why_open: There is no agreed test for understanding and no final definition of it. Programs now pass tests that people once thought needed understanding, and experts still disagree about what that shows.

open_questions.q: Do the radio waves from phones and towers affect small beings such as bees and birds?
open_questions.why_open: Some laboratory studies report changes in how bees behave near strong signals, and others find none. Studies in the open air cannot easily separate radio waves from pesticides, lost nesting places and other changes.

open_questions.q: Why do false stories spread faster than true ones?
open_questions.why_open: The 2018 study showed that they do on one large social site. Surprise seems to be part of the reason. Nobody has yet shown what would slow them without also silencing true stories.

open_questions.q: Why is it easier to be unkind on a screen than face to face?
open_questions.why_open: Psychologists have several ideas: no face to see, a feeling of being hidden, and no answer coming back at once. Studies have not agreed on which matters most.

playtest: Checked: the message without a face test (e1) needs only paper, a pencil and two readers, and about 25 minutes. A fresh secret list and a shuffle for each round stop readers from remembering earlier rounds. Typical results with readers who know the child are 1 to 3 right with the chit, 3 to 5 with the voice and 4 to 6 with the face, against about 2 by pure guessing. A reader who knows the child very well may do well from the words alone, and the step says what to do then. The cup phone (e2) works every time with a tight string of 3 to 4 metres. The step says what to check if it does not. An adult makes the holes. Every activity, project, challenge and the game works with no phone and no internet, and nothing asks a child to go online. A grown-up stays beside the child for anything on a screen. The game works for 1, 2 or 4 players. Facts still to verify before this goes out to families: the Kruger 2005 figures (78 expected and 56 actual), the Vosoughi 2018 figures, the Orben and Przybylski 2019 figure and the potato comparison, the Chang 2015 figure, the Wu 2018 trial size, the Indian Academy of Pediatrics 2021 limit, the helpline numbers 1098, 112 and 1930 and that 112 works on a locked phone, the 2002 resolution on Meucci, Bose's 1895 demonstration and the claim about Marconi's receiver, Hedy Lamarr's 1942 patent, Radia Perlman's 1985 work, the first ARPANET message on 29 October 1969, Martin Cooper's call on 3 April 1973, India's first mobile call on 31 July 1995, India's first telegraph line in 1850, the telegram service closing in July 2013, the cable landing cities, the more than 30 metals and the Congo share of cobalt, the Amnesty 2016 report, Australia's under-16 law of 2024, the 2011 WHO agency grouping, the 2011 Environment Ministry committee, the 2021 UN Committee on the Rights of the Child statement, the Global E-waste Monitor 2024, Jensen's Kerala study years, and the exact verse numbers of the quoted teachings. terms.meaning: A machine that sends your voice, words and pictures to someone far away.
terms.example: You call your grandmother in Madurai on a phone and she hears you at once.
terms.art: A girl talking into a phone with a dotted line to a small house far away.

terms.meaning: A pattern that can travel from one place to another.
terms.example: A phone changes your voice into a signal, sends it, and the other phone changes it back into sound.
terms.art: A wavy line leaving a phone and crossing a hill.

terms.meaning: A tiny part that feels the shaking of your voice in the air.
terms.example: When you speak to a phone, the microphone feels your voice and the phone turns it into a signal.
terms.art: A close picture of a phone's small hole near the bottom, with sound waves going in.

terms.meaning: Things that repeat or follow a plan, so they can be copied.
terms.example: Dot, dash, dot, dash is a pattern. A phone sends your voice as a pattern.
terms.art: A row of dots and dashes in a repeating order.

terms.meaning: A tall metal frame that catches and sends the radio waves of phones.
terms.example: Your phone talks to the nearest mobile tower, and the tower passes the call on.
terms.art: A tall metal tower with flat boxes on top, beside a coconut tree.

terms.meaning: A kind of light that our eyes cannot see. Phones use it to send signals through the air.
terms.example: A phone with no wire sends your call to the tower as radio waves.
terms.art: A phone with curved lines spreading out through a window.

terms.meaning: Radio waves that join a phone to the internet inside a home or a shop.
terms.example: The little box in your house sends Wi-Fi, so the tablet can reach the internet with no wire.

terms.meaning: Millions of computers and phones joined together so they can send messages to each other.
