experiments.title: The message without a face test
experiments.context: In this experiment you write six short messages. Then you see how well people read your feeling from the paper, from your voice, and from your face. No phone is needed.
experiments.question: The same words are written, spoken from behind a door, and said face to face. How much of the feeling do people get right?
experiments.predict: Guess how many of the six feelings a reader will get right in each round. Will the chit, the voice or the face give the most right? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same six messages and the same three feelings are used in every round. Only one thing changes: what the reader can use. In round 1 the reader sees only the chit. In round 2 the reader hears only the voice. In round 3 the reader sees the face and hears the voice. Two readers try every round, because one reader can be lucky. The child makes a new secret list and shuffles the chits before each round, so nobody can remember the last list.

materials.item: 6 small chits of paper, each about the size of a playing card
a pencil
3 small sheets of paper for the secret lists of feelings
a door or a thick curtain to stand behind
2 readers: a grown-up and one more person, such as a brother, sister, grandparent or neighbour
1 sheet of paper for the score table

experiments.record: Draw the table on one sheet. Tick each right guess. Add up each round. Then say or write three things: what I thought, what I saw, and why.

setup.art: A child at a table writing a short word on a small chit of paper, with six chits in a row.
setup.caption: 1. Write one short message on each of 6 chits.

setup.art: A child folding a small paper with six numbered lines and hiding it from a reader who holds one chit.
setup.caption: 2. Keep a secret list of six feelings. Two happy, two upset and two joking.

setup.art: A child standing behind a half-open door saying words while a reader sits on the other side with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 3. Round 2: say the words from behind the door, so only your voice is heard.

setup.art: Two children face to face, one saying words with a big frown and the other pointing to a score table.
setup.caption: 4. Round 3: say the words face to face, and count right guesses for each round.

flow.do: Cut or tear 6 chits of paper. Write one short message on each chit. Use these: Fine. Okay. Come here. Nice shoes. Really? Sure. Put the chits in a pile, face down.
flow.say: Each of these can be said in a happy way, an upset way or a joking way. Try 'Fine.' in all three ways.
flow.kid: Write one message on each chit. Say 'Fine.' in a happy voice. Say it in an upset voice. Say it in a joking voice.
flow.parent: These words are short, so the words alone give little away. Do not use a message such as 'I am so sad', because it names its own feeling.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many right a reader will get in each of the three rounds. Write the guesses at the top of the score sheet.
flow.say: In which round will a reader guess best, the chit, the voice or the face? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which round will be easiest to read, the chit, the voice or the face? Write why.

ask.q: If a reader only guesses, how many of the 6 would be right?
good: About 2, because one choice in three is right.
Not many, because there are three choices.

flow.parent: Do not say who is right. The rounds will answer.

flow.do: Round 1, the chit. Your child makes a secret list on a small paper: numbers 1 to 6, and next to each a feeling. Use happy two times, upset two times and joking two times, in any order. Your child hands reader 1 one chit at a time, face up, and says nothing. Reader 1 says happy, upset or joking. Your child ticks right or wrong on the secret list, without showing it. Then reader 2 does the same, in another room, so reader 2 cannot hear reader 1.
flow.say: Hold up the chit without a word. The reader has only the paper. Do not help with your face.
flow.kid: Make a secret list of six feelings. Show a chit. Say nothing. Tick if the reader is right.
flow.parent: If only one reader is at home, the second reader can be the same person on another day. Use a new secret list. If your child gives hints with the face or voice, remind them that this round is only the paper.

flow.do: Round 2, the voice. Shuffle the chits. Your child makes a new secret list. Your child stands behind the door or curtain, with a reader on the other side. Your child reads out the words of each chit in the feeling on the list. Make the feeling big and clear. The reader guesses and your child ticks. Then reader 2 does the same.
flow.say: Say the words as if you really feel that feeling. The reader cannot see you. What is the reader using now?
flow.kid: Shuffle the chits. Make a new secret list. Stand behind the door. Say each message in its feeling. Tick the right guesses.
flow.parent: Check that the reader cannot see your child through a gap.

flow.do: Round 3, the face and the voice. Shuffle the chits. Your child makes a new secret list. Your child stands in front of the reader and says each message in its feeling, with the face as well. The reader guesses and your child ticks. Then reader 2 does the same.
flow.say: Now the reader has your face as well as your voice. Do you think the number will go up or down?
flow.kid: Shuffle again. Make a new secret list. Say each message to the reader with your face and your voice. Tick the right guesses.
flow.parent: Your child may get giggly in this round. That is fine, but ask them to hold the feeling for one second, so the reader can read it.

flow.do: Add up each round for both readers. Ask your child to say three things: what I thought, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: In which round did the readers get the most right? In which round the fewest? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: Count the ticks in each round. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: The words on the chit never changed. So where did the extra feeling come from in round 2 and round 3?
good: From the voice.
From the face.
The reader put the feeling together from what they heard and saw.

ask.q: What does this test not tell us?
good: How every person would do, because only two readers tried.
Whether a good actor gets more right than a shy child.
Whether emoji or a voice note would help.

check.q: A reader gets 2 right on the chit round and 5 right on the voice round. What most likely helped?
check.why: The words stayed the same, so the extra feeling must have come from the voice. Choosing luck means counting one round as proof, so repeat with a second reader to check.

flow.parent: Typical results with two readers who know your child are 1 to 3 right for the chit, 3 to 5 for the voice and 4 to 6 for the face. Pure guessing gives about 2. Your numbers will differ, because a reader who knows your child well may do well even from the words. That is also a finding, so write it down. If the chit gets 5 or 6 right, the voice and face rounds will still usually score the same or higher.
flow.think: You can fix a message that is easy to misread. What could you add to a typed 'Fine.' so that your cousin reads it as you meant it?

experiments.title: The cup phone: does the string need to be tight?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a cup-and-string phone and test when a whisper gets through. It shows that a voice is shaking that can travel along a string.
experiments.question: Does the string of a cup phone have to be tight for a whisper to get through?
experiments.predict: Guess what happens if the string is tight, loose, or held by a finger in the middle. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same two cups, the same string, the same three words and the same quiet voice are used every time. Only the string changes: tight, loose, then pinched by a finger. Each way is tried three times with three different words, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 2 paper or plastic cups, or 2 clean empty curd cups
about 4 metres of cotton string or kite thread
2 buttons or 2 short sticks, to stop the string slipping out
a pencil with a sharp point, for an adult to make the holes
a quiet room or corridor with 4 metres of clear space
a partner to listen

experiments.safety: An adult makes the holes in the cups, because a pencil point is sharp and can slip.
experiments.record: Draw the table. In each box, write a tick if the word was clear. Write a half tick if it was faint, and a cross if it was not heard. Then say or write what I thought, what I saw, and why.

setup.art: A grown-up pushing a pencil point through the middle of the bottom of a paper cup, with the child watching.
setup.caption: 1. An adult makes a small hole in the middle of the bottom of each cup.

setup.art: A string passing through two cups, each with a button knotted inside the cup so the string cannot pull out.
setup.caption: 2. Thread one end into each cup, and knot it around a button inside.

setup.art: Two children stretching the string straight between two cups, one speaking into the cup and the other pressing the cup to an ear.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the string straight and tight. One speaks, one listens.

setup.art: The same two children with the string sagging in a curve, then a third picture with a finger pinching the string.
setup.caption: 4. Try again with the string loose, and again with a finger pinching it.

flow.do: An adult pokes a small hole in the middle of the bottom of each cup. Thread one end of the string through each hole. Tie each end around a button inside the cup, with a double knot, so it cannot pull out.
flow.say: These two cups are going to be a phone. There is no battery and no tower. What do you think will carry the voice?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make the holes. Thread the string and tie each end round a button inside the cup.
flow.parent: If you use thin thread, double it. Cotton string works best. If the string slips out, use a bigger button or tie a knot around a small stick.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before any test. Write the guess on the record sheet.
flow.say: Will the voice get through if the string is loose? What about if a finger pinches the string? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the voice get through if the string is tight, loose, or pinched? Write why.
flow.parent: Do not say who is right. The cups will answer.

flow.do: Stand about 4 metres apart. Pull the string straight, so it is tight and does not touch anything. The speaker holds the cup near the mouth and whispers three different words, one at a time. The listener presses the other cup gently on an ear and says each word back. Write a tick, a half tick or a cross for each word.
flow.say: Whisper slowly. The listener says back every word. Does the voice get through on a tight string?
flow.kid: Pull the string tight. One person whispers three words. The other listens and says them back. Tick what was heard.
flow.parent: If nothing is heard even on the tight string, check four things. The knots should hold. The string should be straight and touching nothing. The cups should not be squashed. If it still fails, shorten the string to 3 metres. Whisper, and do not shout, because shouting does not help.

flow.do: Now let the string sag a little, in a curve, and do the same thing with three different words. Write a tick, a half tick or a cross for each.
flow.say: Is the voice as clear on a loose string? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Let the string go loose. Whisper three more words. Tick what is heard.

ask.q: What do you think is happening inside the string when the voice gets through?
good: The string is shaking.
The shaking of the voice runs along the string.
The cup shakes the string and the string shakes the other cup.

flow.parent: Expect faint or no sound on a loose string. A loose string cannot pass the shaking along well.

flow.do: Pull the string tight again. A third person, or the speaker with the free hand, pinches the string in the middle between two fingers. Whisper three words. Write what is heard.
flow.say: Now the string is tight, but a finger is holding it. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Pinch the middle of the tight string. Whisper three words. Tick what is heard.
flow.parent: Expect the voice to stop or become very faint. A finger stops the string from shaking.

flow.do: Look at the table. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which way worked best? What does a string do for a voice?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw and why.

ask.q: A mobile phone has no string. What does it use instead to carry a voice through the air?
good: Radio waves.
Invisible waves, like light that we cannot see.

check.q: A cup phone works with a tight string and not with a pinched string. What does that show?
options: The voice travels as shaking along the string
The string is magic when tight
check.why: A finger stops the string from shaking, and the voice stops with it. Choosing magic means the shaking was not noticed, so touch the tight string while someone whispers, and feel it hum.

flow.parent: This test cannot tell how a mobile phone works. A mobile phone turns the voice into a pattern and sends it by radio waves. It does show that a voice can travel as shaking.
flow.think: Try the cups with a longer string. How long can you make the string before the whisper stops getting through?

activities.title: Send a drawing in packets
activities.context: In this activity you cut a drawing into numbered pieces. You send the pieces by different roads and put the drawing together again. It shows how a photo travels on the internet.

materials.item: 1 sheet of paper and colour pencils or crayons
scissors, for a grown-up to use or to help with
a second person, to be the other phone

schedule.what: Draw, cut into 8 pieces, number them, send them by different roads, and put the drawing together.

activities.record: Draw the 8 numbered pieces in the order they arrived, then draw the finished picture. Write which piece was late.

setup.art: A child drawing a mango on a sheet of paper with colour pencils.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big, simple picture on one sheet.

setup.art: The same drawing cut into eight pieces, each with a number and a small address written on the back.
setup.caption: 2. Cut it into 8 pieces. Write 1 to 8 on the back of each, and your friend's name.

setup.art: Pieces of paper travelling by three different roads across the floor to a second child, who puts them together in order.
setup.caption: 3. Send the pieces by three roads. Your friend puts them back in order.

flow.do: Draw a big, simple picture on a sheet, such as a mango with a leaf. Colour it. Fold the sheet in half three times to make 8 parts and cut along the folds. On the back of each piece, write a number from 1 to 8. Also write the name of the person who will receive it. Mix the pieces.
flow.say: A photo on a phone is cut into many small pieces like this. Each piece has an address and a number.
flow.kid: Draw a picture. Cut it into 8 pieces. Write 1 to 8 on the back, and a name.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts if the child is under 8, or the child cuts with blunt scissors.

flow.do: Put three paper routes on the floor with chappals or books. One road goes straight across the room, one goes around the sofa, and one goes the long way round the table. Send the pieces to the second person, a few pieces by each road. Pieces arrive in a mixed order.
flow.say: Some roads are long and some are short. Do the pieces arrive in the order you sent them?
flow.kid: Send three pieces by each road. They will arrive in a mixed order.

ask.q: Why does each piece have a number?
good: So the pieces can be put back in order.
Because they arrive in a different order from the order they were sent.

flow.do: The second person puts the pieces in order by the numbers and rebuilds the picture. Then do it again, but one piece is held back and never arrives. Ask the second person to say which number is missing and to ask for that piece again.
flow.say: Can you tell which piece is missing without seeing it? What does the phone do when a packet is lost?
flow.kid: Put the pieces in order. One is missing. Say its number and ask for it again.
flow.parent: A phone really does this. It notices the number that is missing and asks for that packet again.
flow.think: If every piece had no number, could you still build the picture? How?

activities.title: Who may know this? A sorting game
activities.context: In this activity you sort twelve facts about a child into three piles, to decide who may know each one. It shows which facts are private.

materials.item: 12 small slips of paper and a pencil
3 sheets of paper to be the piles

schedule.what: Write the 12 slips, sort them into 3 piles, and talk about the ones you put in different places.

activities.record: Draw three boxes and write each slip in the box where it belongs. Colour the box 'Nobody except my parent' red.

setup.art: Twelve slips of paper in a row, each with a short fact about a child, such as 'my home address' or 'my favourite food'.
setup.caption: 1. Write one fact on each of 12 slips.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper labelled Anyone I meet, My family and trusted adults, and Nobody except my parent.
setup.caption: 2. Put three sheets on the table, with these three names.

setup.art: A child placing a slip on one of the three sheets while a parent watches.
setup.caption: 3. Place each slip in the pile you think it belongs to, and say why.

flow.do: Write these 12 facts on 12 slips, one on each. My favourite food. My first name. My pet's name. My full name. My home address. My school's name. My phone number. My password. A photo of me in school uniform. My birthday date. The one-time password a bank sent. My favourite cartoon.
flow.say: Some of these are like the key to your house. Some are just things you like. Let us find which is which.
flow.kid: Write one fact on each of the 12 slips.
flow.parent: Read each slip aloud for a younger child. Mix them before sorting.

flow.do: Lay three sheets on the table. The first sheet says: Anyone I meet. The second says: My family and trusted adults. The third says: Nobody except my parent. Your child puts each slip on a sheet and says why. Do not correct yet.
flow.say: Who may know your home address? Who may know your favourite food? Why do you put it there?
flow.kid: Put each slip on a sheet. Say why.

ask.q: Why is a password in a different pile from a favourite food?
good: A password opens an account, so a stranger could use it.
A favourite food cannot lead anyone to me.

flow.parent: Answers that differ from ours are worth listening to. The main idea: a fact goes with the people who need it. A favourite food or a pet's name is low risk. A home address, a school and a photo in uniform lead a stranger to your child. A password and a one-time password are for a parent or for nobody.

flow.do: Now look at the 'Anyone I meet' pile together. Ask whether any slip in it could help a stranger find your child. Move any that could. Then say which pile a slip such as 'my full name' belongs in when it is combined with 'my school's name'.
flow.say: One small fact is harmless. What happens when a stranger collects several?
flow.kid: Look at the first pile. Could any slip there help a stranger find you? Move it.
flow.think: Is there a fact you want to keep for your family that is not on the slips?

activities.title: Stop, do not answer, keep it, tell
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up writes pretend messages on paper slips. The child practises four steps for when something feels wrong. No phone is used.

materials.item: 4 slips of paper with messages written by the grown-up
a pencil
a box or an envelope, to be the 'keep it' place

schedule.what: Practise the four steps with four pretend messages, and make the hand signs.

activities.record: Draw four small pictures in a row for the four steps. Draw a raised hand for stop, a closed mouth, a message in a box, and a child showing a grown-up.

setup.art: A grown-up writing a pretend message on a slip of paper, such as 'You won a prize, press here'.
setup.caption: 1. The grown-up writes four pretend messages on slips.

setup.art: A child holding up a hand to say stop, then a finger on closed lips.
setup.caption: 2. The child reads a slip and does two hand signs: stop, then do not answer.

setup.art: A child dropping the slip into an envelope and then walking to a grown-up with the envelope.
setup.caption: 3. The child keeps the slip and takes it to a trusted adult.

flow.do: Write four pretend messages on four slips. Use these. 'You have won a phone! Press here.' 'I am eight too. What is your address?' 'Send me your photo. Keep this our secret.' 'Read me the number the bank sent you.' Then teach the four steps with hand signs. Use a flat hand for stop and a finger on the lips for do not answer. Use a slip put in an envelope for keep it, and a hand pointing to a grown-up for tell.
flow.say: When a message feels wrong, we do four things. Stop. Do not answer. Keep it. Tell a trusted adult. Let us practise.
flow.kid: Learn the four signs: stop, finger on lips, put it in the envelope, point to a grown-up.
flow.parent: Keep your voice calm. The aim is that your child knows what to do, not that they feel frightened.

flow.do: Hand your child one slip at a time, as if it arrived on a screen. Your child does the four steps with the hand signs and puts the slip in the envelope. Then your child hands you the envelope and says, 'Something on the phone scared me. Please look at it with me.' Reply warmly and thank them for telling you. Do this for all four slips.
flow.say: Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing. You are never in trouble for telling.
flow.kid: Read a slip. Make the signs. Put it in the envelope. Say the words to a grown-up.

ask.q: Why do we keep the message and not delete it?
good: The grown-up needs to see it.
It helps find who sent it.

ask.q: What do we say to the grown-up?
good: Something scared me. Please look with me.

flow.parent: Do not scold, however the slip was reached. Children tell more often when they are sure that telling will not bring a punishment.

flow.do: Now the child writes one more slip, a message that would make them feel strange. They hand it to you. You do the four steps this time, and the child says 'Thank you for telling me.'
flow.say: You write a message that would feel wrong, and I will do the four steps.
flow.kid: Write a pretend message that feels wrong. Give it to a grown-up. Watch them do the four steps.
flow.think: Who are the trusted adults for you? Name three.

activities.title: Believe it or check it?
activities.context: In this activity you sort six claims into 'believe' or 'check first', by asking two questions. It shows how to handle things that you hear on a screen.

materials.item: 6 slips of paper with claims written on them
a pencil

schedule.what: Read six claims, ask two questions of each, and sort them.

activities.record: Draw two boxes called Believe and Check first. Write the number of each claim in its box.

setup.art: Six slips of paper, each with a short claim, laid out in two rows on a table.
setup.caption: 1. The grown-up writes six claims on six slips.

setup.art: A child holding a magnifying-glass drawing over a slip, with two question marks above it.
setup.caption: 2. For each slip, ask: who is saying this? How do they know?

setup.art: Two boxes on a table, Believe and Check first, with slips placed in each.
setup.caption: 3. Put each slip in a box.

flow.do: Write these six claims on six slips. 1. Your grandmother says: 'I saw the rain start on the terrace this morning.' 2. A message that has been forwarded many times says: 'School is closed tomorrow. Send to ten people.' 3. A picture on a screen shows a huge fish in a village pond, with no name or place. 4. Your neighbour says: 'The bus stop moved. I walked past it today.' 5. A message says: 'Tell nobody. Press here to win money.' 6. A cousin says: 'I heard that the new shop gives free sweets.'
flow.say: Some things we can believe because the speaker saw them. Some things we should check first. Let us find out which is which.
flow.kid: Write the six claims on slips.
flow.parent: The claims are made up. Read each one slowly for a younger child.

flow.do: Take one slip at a time. Ask your child two questions out loud: Who is saying this? How do they know? Your child decides if the slip goes in Believe or Check first, and says why.
flow.say: Who is saying this? How do they know? Did they see it themselves?
flow.kid: Read a slip. Ask: who is saying this? How do they know? Put the slip in a box.

ask.q: What do you do with a message that says 'Send this to ten people quickly'?
good: Check it first.
Ask a grown-up.
Do not send it, because it asks me to skip the checking.

flow.parent: Slips 1 and 4 are believable, because the speaker saw it and is close to you. Slips 2, 3, 5 and 6 need checking. Slip 6 is worth checking because the cousin only heard it. Slip 5 is also a trick.

flow.do: Ask your child to make up one claim for you. You ask the two questions, and your child answers whether you should believe it.
flow.say: Now you make up a claim and I will ask the two questions.
flow.kid: Make up a claim for a grown-up. Listen to the two questions.
flow.think: Is a thing true because many people say it?

projects.title: Our family's phone and screen rules
projects.context: In this project, over three days, your family makes a place for the phone to sleep. It also tries a habit that rests the eyes, and makes a promise card about telling. Nothing needs a phone.

materials.item: a card or half a sheet of thick paper for the Phone's Home sign
colour pencils or pens
a clock or a kitchen timer, and a book or paper for drawing
a window with a far view, such as a tree or a tower
2 more cards for the Promise Card, and a pencil

schedule.what: Make the Phone's Home sign and choose a sleeping place outside the bedroom.
Try the 20 minutes, 20 seconds habit for resting the eyes.
Make the Promise Card with three trusted adults and the helpline numbers.

projects.record: Keep the sign, a drawing of what you saw from the window on day 2, and the Promise Card. On day 3, say which of the three habits you want to keep.

setup.art: A card sign with the words 'Phone's Home' and a drawing of a phone sleeping in a small basket on a shelf.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: make a sign and choose a shelf outside the bedroom for the phone to sleep.

setup.art: A child drawing at a table, with a window behind showing a far-off coconut tree, and a timer showing 20 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: draw or read for 20 minutes, then look at the farthest thing for 20 seconds.

setup.art: A hand-drawn Promise Card with three names, the numbers 1098 and 112, and a heart.
setup.caption: 3. Day 3: make a Promise Card with trusted adults' names and helplines.

flow.do: Choose a place outside the bedroom where the family's phones can sleep at night. A shelf, a basket or a steel tin in the hall will do. Make a card sign that says 'Phone's Home' and decorate it. Put it up. Agree who will put the phone there each night, and at what time.
flow.say: A bright screen late at night tells your body that it is still day, and it holds back sleep. Where should the phones sleep?
flow.kid: Make a Phone's Home sign. Put it where the phones sleep.
flow.parent: Every person in the family, including the grown-ups, puts their phone there. A rule that applies to everyone is easier to keep.

flow.do: Set a timer for 20 minutes. Your child draws or reads a book, which are both near work for the eyes. When the timer rings, they look out of the window at the farthest thing they can see for 20 seconds. Count slowly. Your child draws what they saw.
flow.say: Your eye has tiny muscles that squeeze to look at near things. After 20 minutes, they need a rest. Looking far gives them one.
flow.kid: Draw for 20 minutes. Then look at the farthest thing for 20 seconds. Draw what you saw.

ask.q: What is the farthest thing you can see from your window?
good: A tree, a tower, a cloud or a hill. Any far thing is right.

flow.parent: Eye doctors call this the 20-20-20 habit. The name counts 20 minutes, 20 feet and 20 seconds. Twenty feet is about 6 metres, so any thing farther than that works. Outdoor daylight also helps children's eyes.

flow.do: Make a Promise Card. Write this on it. 'If you tell me about something scary on a screen, I will not be angry. I will not take the phone away because you told me.' The grown-up signs it. The child writes the names of three trusted adults. Both add the numbers: Childline 1098 for a child who needs help, and 112 for any emergency.
flow.say: This is a promise from me to you. You will never be punished for telling me. Who are three people you can tell?
flow.kid: Write three names of trusted adults on the card. Add 1098 and 112.
flow.parent: Many children do not tell, because they fear the phone will be taken away. This promise answers that fear before it starts. Keep the card where your child can see it. The cyber helpline for money tricks on the phone is 1930, for the grown-ups to keep.
flow.think: Which of these three habits is the easiest for us to keep? Which is the hardest?

challenges.title: A family code word
challenges.context: This is a design problem. Someone you do not know says that a family member sent them to fetch you. You design a way for a child to know if that is true, using no phone at all.
challenges.problem: Design a way for a child to know if a message or a person really comes from the family. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: It must work with no phone or internet.
A seven-year-old must be able to remember it easily.
A stranger must not be able to guess it or find it written down.
It must be possible to change it when someone has said it aloud.
materials: a grown-up to play the stranger

setup.art: A grown-up at a door saying 'Your mother sent me', with a child looking up at them with a thoughtful face.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up plays a person who says the family sent them.

setup.art: A child and a parent whispering a word to each other at a table, with a sketch of a key beside them.
setup.caption: 2. The family chooses a secret code word together.

setup.art: A child asking the pretend stranger 'What is the word?' with a hand held up.
setup.caption: 3. The child asks for the code word. The family test begins.

flow.do: The grown-up plays a person at the door. The person says, 'Your mother sent me to pick you up.' Ask your child how to find out if it is true. Let them think of two ideas without help.
flow.say: A person says your family sent them. How could you find out if it is true?
flow.kid: Think of two ways to check that a person really comes from your family.

ask.q: Why is a name or a smiling face not enough?
good: Anyone can say a name.
A kind face does not prove anything.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Let your child struggle for a moment, because the struggle shows why the problem is real.

flow.do: Together, work out three ways. A code word known only to the family. A question that only the family can answer, such as 'What did Grandmother put in the curd rice?'. A rule that the child never goes with anyone without first asking a trusted adult in the building. Choose one and write it on a paper, in a place the stranger cannot see. Test it by letting the grown-up play the stranger and ask the child to check.
flow.say: The stranger does not know our word. How will you ask?
flow.kid: Choose a code word with a grown-up. Practise asking: What is the word?
flow.parent: A code word should be a word that nobody would guess, not a name or a school. Keep it away from any message or photo. Change it if it is ever said aloud.

flow.do: Now try the creative ways. Make up a code question and a hand sign, such as touching an ear. Test them with the pretend stranger. Then ask your child to say what they will do if the pretend stranger gets the word wrong.
flow.say: What do you do if the stranger gets the word wrong?
flow.kid: Test your code. If the word is wrong, say no, walk away and tell a trusted adult.
flow.think: Is a code word still safe after you have said it aloud near other people?

general: A code word that only the family knows, changed when it has been said near a stranger.
A question that only the family can answer, such as the name of a family pet.
A rule that the child goes with nobody until a trusted adult they know has said yes face to face.
creative: A code that changes every week. A different member of the family chooses it each time, so choosing is a game.
A pair of words, one said by the child and one by the person, like a lock and key.
A drawn symbol that the person must show, made on a card that the child keeps inside a shoe.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own way to know that a person comes from your family. Who would you tell about it? What would you do if the word was said out loud near a stranger?

challenges.title: A message that cannot be misread
challenges.context: This is a design problem. You find a way to write 'Fine.' on a chit so that the reader gets your feeling right. You use only paper and pencils.
challenges.problem: Write the word 'Fine.' on a chit so that a reader gets your feeling right. The feeling is happy, upset or joking. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only a chit of paper and a pencil.
No more than five words and one small drawing.
The reader must not hear your voice or see your face.
Test your chit on at least two readers, and count their right guesses.

setup.art: A single chit with 'Fine.' written on it and three question marks over it.
setup.caption: 1. Begin with a plain 'Fine.' chit and find out how many readers get it right.

setup.art: A second chit with 'Fine, I am happy!' and a small smiling face drawn on it.
setup.caption: 2. Make a new chit with a feeling word and a small drawing.

setup.art: Two readers each looking at a chit and holding up a happy, upset or joking card.
setup.caption: 3. Test the new chit on two readers. Count right guesses.

flow.do: Choose a feeling in secret. Write a plain 'Fine.' on a chit. Hand it to two readers, one at a time, and ask each to say happy, upset or joking. Write down how many were right. Do this for each of the three feelings if you have time.
flow.say: A plain word has no feeling in it. How many readers got your feeling right?
flow.kid: Write 'Fine.' on a chit. Choose a feeling in secret. Test two readers. Count the right guesses.
flow.parent: Expect about one reader in three to be right by luck.

flow.do: Now change the chit so that the feeling is clear. Let the child try their own ideas. They might add a feeling word, a small face, a question, or a reason. Test it on the same two readers, with a fresh feeling. Count the right guesses again.
flow.say: What can you add so that the reader does not have to guess?
flow.kid: Add a word, a face or a reason to your chit. Test it on two readers.

ask.q: What did you add, and did it help?
good: A feeling word.
A small face.
A reason, such as 'Fine, I am just tired'.

flow.do: Compare the plain chit with the new one. Ask your child which change helped most. Then ask whether any chit can ever carry all of the feeling, as a face and voice can.
flow.say: Is your new chit as clear as your voice?
flow.kid: Compare. Which change helped most?
flow.think: If you could add one thing to every message you send, what would it be?

general: Add a feeling word, such as 'Fine, I am happy!'.
Add a small drawing of a face.
Add a reason, such as 'Fine, I was only tired', so the reader knows why.
creative: Make a set of three colour dots that the family agrees on: red for cross, yellow for joking, green for happy.
Write the message and then draw your own face saying it, like a speech bubble.
Send two chits together: the word, and a second chit that says how you feel.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own way to put feeling into a written message. Would your way work with someone who has never seen your colours or faces? How could you check?

games.title: Go Ahead, Ask First or Stop and Tell: a card game
games.context: This is a card game. Each player decides what to do about a made-up situation with a phone, and the group talks about the best answer. It practises how to guard against misuse.

setup.art: 16 situation cards and 3 answer cards for each player, laid out on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 16 situation cards and 3 answer cards for each player.

setup.art: Two players each holding three answer cards face down, with a pile of situation cards between them.
setup.caption: 2. Each player takes a set of three answer cards. Shuffle the situation cards.

setup.art: Two players placing one answer card each face down on the table after a card is read aloud.
setup.caption: 3. Read a card. Each player secretly picks one answer, then turns it over together.

items.f: A message from a number you do not know says, 'You have won a phone! Press here.'
items.b: STOP AND TELL. Do not press the link. Keep the message and show a grown-up. A prize that asks you to press a link is a trick.

items.f: A person in a game says, 'I am eight like you. Keep this our secret.'
items.b: STOP AND TELL. You cannot see who is typing. A person who says 'Keep this our secret' is giving a clear sign to tell a trusted adult.

items.f: You want to send your friend's dancing video to your cousin.
items.b: ASK FIRST. Ask your friend, and not only yourself. A person decides about their own picture.

items.f: You want to download a new game.
items.b: ASK FIRST. Ask a grown-up, because a game can have a link that does harm or cost real money.

items.f: A grown-up is beside you. You want to send your drawing of a peacock to your grandmother.
items.b: GO AHEAD. Your own drawing, with a grown-up beside you, sent to someone you know, is fine.

items.f: Someone calls and says, 'I am from the bank. Read me the number that just came to your phone.'
items.b: STOP AND TELL. A real bank never asks for that number. Give the phone to a grown-up.

items.f: Three friends have a group that makes fun of a classmate who stammers.
items.b: STOP AND TELL. Do not pass it on. Say a kind word to the classmate, and tell a trusted adult. Bullying done again and again is hurtful.

items.f: You typed 'Fine.' to your cousin and you are not sure how she will read it.
items.b: TWO ANSWERS ARE GOOD. You can go ahead after adding a feeling word, such as 'Fine, happy!'. Or you can call her instead, so she hears your voice. Sending it unchanged risks a wrong reading.

items.f: You find a phone on the road.
items.b: STOP AND TELL. Do not open it. Give it to a grown-up, so that it can go back to its owner.
ASK FIRST. Coins cost real money from a real bank account. A grown-up decides.

items.f: A forwarded message says, 'Send this to ten people in one minute or you will have bad luck.'
items.b: ASK FIRST. A message that asks you to rush is asking you to skip the checking. Ask who says it and how they know.

items.f: Someone filmed a classmate crying and wants you to forward it, because it is funny.
items.b: STOP AND TELL. Do not forward it. Forwarding makes more copies that cannot be taken back. Tell a trusted adult.

items.f: You ask a talking speaker for the way to a temple and it gives a long answer.
items.b: ASK FIRST. A speaker is a program and can be wrong while sounding sure. Check with a grown-up who knows the way.

items.f: Your cousin sends a silly joke picture. You want to reply with a big laugh.
items.b: TWO ANSWERS ARE GOOD. You can go ahead, because a friendly reply to a cousin is kind. You can also call to laugh together, so she hears the laugh. Both are good.

items.f: Your uncle's phone buzzes with a message, and it is lying next to you.
items.b: ASK FIRST. Reading someone else's messages without asking is misuse, even at home. Ask first or leave it.

items.f: A message says, 'I am your aunt's friend. Tell me your school name and I will bring a gift.'
items.b: STOP AND TELL. A school name is private information. Do not answer. Keep the message and show a trusted adult.

printables.title: 3 answer cards for each player (make one set for every player)

items.b: Fine to do. A grown-up is beside you and you know the person.
Ask a grown-up, or ask the person in the picture, before you do anything.
Stop. Do not answer. Keep it. Tell a trusted adult the same day.

rules: Every player has 3 answer cards: GO AHEAD, ASK FIRST and STOP AND TELL. Shuffle the 16 situation cards and put them in a pile, face down.
One player is the reader. The reader turns over the top card and reads the front aloud. The other players, and the reader too, each put one answer card face down on the table.
Everyone turns their card over together. Each player says in one sentence why they chose it.

The reader turns the card over and reads the back aloud. A player whose answer matches the back scores 1 point. A player whose answer is different, but who gives a good reason that the group accepts, also scores 1 point.
On a card that says TWO ANSWERS ARE GOOD, either of the two answers on the back scores a point. An answer not named on the back scores nothing.

The next player becomes the reader. The game ends when all 16 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If you play as a team, the shared goal is to score 24 points together out of a possible 32.
If you play alone, read each card, choose an answer, then check the back. Count your points out of 16.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 situation cards. Cut out one set of 3 answer cards for every player. Shuffle the situation cards. Read the three answers together.
flow.say: We will read a situation, and each choose what to do. There are three answers. Which of them is the one that you would use for a message that scares you?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Learn the three answers: go ahead, ask first, stop and tell.
flow.parent: Cut out the cards for a younger child. Keep them in an envelope for next time.

flow.do: Play 16 rounds. In each round, one player reads a situation aloud. Everyone chooses an answer in secret and shows it together. Then the reader reads the back. Talk about any answer that was different.
flow.say: What did you choose? Why? What does the back say?
flow.kid: Read a card. Choose an answer. Show it. Read the back. Count your points.
flow.parent: If an answer was different from the back, ask why. A child's reason may show a good point. The back shows the safest answer.

flow.do: Count the points and say who has won. Then ask which card was the hardest, and why. Put the cards away.
flow.say: Which card was the hardest? Which one would you change?
flow.kid: Count your points. Say which card was the hardest.
flow.think: What would you add if you could write a seventeenth situation card?

worksheets.title: Phones, messages and staying safe (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks the main ideas of how a phone works and what to do when something on a screen feels wrong.

items.p: Which of these carries internet messages between countries?
opts: Cables under the sea
Wires in the clouds
Flying birds
items.why: Glass threads in thick cables lie on the sea floor and carry messages as flashes of light. If you chose clouds, remember that the 'cloud' is really buildings of computers.

items.p: True or false: it is fine to tell your best friend your password.
items.a: false
items.why: A password is shared only with your parent. A best friend today may not be a best friend next month.

items.p: When something on a screen scares you, you stop, do not answer, keep it and ____ a trusted adult.
items.a: tell
items.why: Telling is the step that brings help. It is never your fault, so tell the same day.

items.p: Sort each one: fine to say to a new friend in person, or private?
items.a: as given
items.why: A favourite game or a pet's name cannot lead a stranger to you. An address, a school and a password can lead a stranger to you or into your account.

items.p: Match each part to what it does.
pairs: feels your voice shaking the air
carries messages as flashes of light
items.a: as given
items.why: The microphone starts the message, the tower catches the radio waves, and the cable carries the message across the sea. Each part has its own job.

items.p: Put the four steps for a scary message in order.
items.why: You stop first so that you do not act in a hurry. You do not answer so that the sender learns nothing. You keep the message so that the adult can see it. Then you tell, the same day.

items.p: A cousin might read 'Come here' as cross. What can you add so that she knows you are happy?
items.a: A good answer adds the feeling in one way. It might be 'Come here, I am so happy!', a smiling face, a voice note, or a call.
items.why: The words alone carry no feeling. Anything that adds your voice, your face or your reason puts some feeling back.

items.p: Draw how a voice goes from one phone to another. Show a microphone, a tower and a second phone.
items.a: A phone with sound waves going in, wavy lines to a tower, a cable to a second tower, and curved lines to a second phone with sound coming out.
items.why: The voice becomes a pattern, travels by radio waves and cables, and becomes sound again at the other end.

items.p: Two views about children and phones.

views.says: A child does not need a phone. Children play outdoors and talk to people face to face.
A phone lets a child call home if lost, and call a grandparent far away.

items.ask: What is good in each view? Would you answer differently for a child who lives far from grandparents?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer finds something true in both views. Outdoor play matters, and a phone can call for help. A rule can keep both.
items.why: Both views are about real needs. A phone helps with calls and emergencies, and a child also needs play, sleep and time with people.

items.p: A funny photo is of your friend. She has not said yes. What do you do before sending it?
opts: Ask her first
Send it. She will laugh later
Send it to only one person
items.why: A photo of a person is their own piece. Even one copy can be passed on. Choosing to send it assumes that a laugh is the same as a yes.

worksheets.title: Copies, tricks and checking (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to explain why messages are misread, why copies cannot be taken back and how to check what you see.

items.p: Why can a typed 'Nice haircut.' hurt, even if you meant it kindly?
opts: The reader may take it as unkind without your smile
The phone changes jokes into rude words
Words on screens are always rude
items.why: The reader has only the letters and has to guess the feeling. A smile, a voice or a kind word puts the feeling back.

items.p: True or false: if you delete a sent message, every copy is gone.
items.a: false
items.why: Deleting removes only your own copy. A friend may have read it, saved it or taken a picture of the screen.

items.p: Which question helps most when checking a message?
opts: Who is saying this, and how do they know?
How many people have forwarded it?
Is it written in capital letters?
items.why: A person who saw or knows a thing is better than a thing that many people have passed on. Many forwards can mean only that it is surprising.

items.p: A phone cuts a photo into small numbered pieces called ____.
items.a: packets
items.why: Each packet has an address and a number, so the pieces can be put back in order.

items.p: Put in order how a photo goes from a phone to a cousin's phone.
a: The phone cuts the photo into packets
Radio waves carry the packets to a tower
The cousin's phone puts the packets back in order
items.why: The photo is cut first, then sent by radio waves to a tower, then carried by cables, and rebuilt at the end by the numbers.

items.p: Match each trick to the best answer.
pairs: 'I am from your bank. Read me the number.'
Never say it. Tell an adult.
Do not press. Show a grown-up.
Say no and tell an adult.
items.a: as given
items.why: Each trick tries to make you act fast or keep quiet. The answer slows you down and brings in an adult.

items.p: A message says 'Send this to ten friends or have bad luck.' Write two questions to ask before you do anything.
items.a: A good answer asks who is saying this and how they know. It may also ask if a grown-up can check it, or why it wants me to hurry.
items.why: A message that asks you to hurry is asking you to skip the checking. Two questions slow you down.

items.p: In two boxes, draw a phone helping someone and the same phone harming someone.
items.a: One box with a help, such as a call to an ambulance, a weather warning to fishing boats or a video call to a grandparent. One box with a harm, such as a cruel message or a scary stranger.
items.why: The same tool does both, so the way that it is used decides.

items.p: Two views about screen time.

views.says: Keep screen time under two hours a day for a child, so that play, sleep and family time come first.
What the child does on the screen matters more than the hours. A video call with a grandparent is not the same as videos alone.

items.ask: Which view would you use for a video call with your grandmother? Is either wrong?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer sees that neither view is wrong. A family might use both a limit on hours and a judgement about what is done.
items.why: Scientists still argue about how much harm screens do. Time and kind of use both seem to matter, so no view is marked right.

items.p: A game wants your address to 'unlock a prize'. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Type it quickly
Ask a grown-up first
Type a made-up address
items.why: Most games do not need an address. A grown-up can say if the game is safe. Typing a made-up one still tells the game that you will hand over facts.

worksheets.title: Weighing words and sharing (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to think about tests, secrets, sharing and the choices a phone gives you.

items.p: A reader gets 2 of 6 right from a chit, 4 from a voice, 6 from a face. What does this suggest?
opts: Voice and face add feeling that words lack
Kavya got better at acting each time
The reader was tired in round 1
items.why: The words stayed the same, so the rise suggests the voice and face added something. Acting and tiredness could matter too, which is why a second reader and a new list are used.

items.p: True or false: a false story always travels slower than a true one.
items.a: false
items.why: In a large study of a social site, false stories reached people faster than true ones, mainly because they felt new and surprising.

items.p: A stranger told your friend, 'Do not tell anyone or you will be in trouble.' What would you tell her?
items.a: A good answer says she should tell a trusted adult and keep the message. It says it is not her fault. It says a stranger who asks for secrecy is giving a clear warning.
items.why: A person who wants a child to keep quiet does not want an adult to see. Telling is the strongest thing a child can do.

items.p: Anil's cousin dares him to share a classmate's embarrassing photo as a joke. What is right?
opts: Share it. It is only a joke
Do not share it, and tell a trusted adult
Share it, then delete it in a minute
items.why: Deleting your copy does not delete the copies already made. A joke that makes one person cry is bullying.

items.p: You send a photo to 3 cousins. Each sends it to 3 others. How many phones hold it, counting yours?
items.why: 1 phone + 3 cousins + 3 × 3 = 9 others. 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. Each round of forwarding multiplies the copies.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Screen lock, asking first, sharing a password, switching off at night.
items.a: Sharing a password, because the other three guard a device and sharing a password gives its guard away.
items.why: A guard keeps others out. Sharing a password lets another person in.

items.p: Sort each one: does it help, or does it harm?
items: a weather warning to a fishing boat
leaving a child out of a group on purpose
a video call with a grandparent
items.a: as given
items.why: The same phone does all five. What it does depends on what a person chooses to do with it.

items.p: Explain to a younger child how a phone with no wire still sends your voice.
items.a: A good answer says the voice is changed into a signal. Radio waves carry it to a tower, and cables carry it on. The other phone changes it back to sound.
items.why: Explaining in your own words shows the idea. The steps are voice, signal, radio waves, tower, cable, signal, voice.

items.p: Two views about posting a child's photo.

views.says: I share the photo out of love, so that relatives far away can see the child growing.
It is a picture of me. Please ask me before you share it.

items.ask: Whose wish should count most? Can both be kept?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says the child's wish matters, because the picture is of them. Both can be kept if the grandparent asks and shares only with people the family knows.
items.why: Children have a right to privacy about their own picture, and love is a reason to share. Asking is a way to hold both.

items.p: Draw a message's road to a cousin's phone in Kochi. Show a tower, a cable and the sea.
items.a: A phone, a tower with wavy lines, a cable going along the ground and under the sea, another coast at Kochi, a tower and a second phone.
items.why: A message goes as radio waves to a tower, then as light along cables under the sea, then as radio waves to the second phone.

quiz.p: A girl speaks into a phone. What does the phone send to her friend?
opts: Her real voice, made louder
A pattern made from her voice
A tiny copy of her body
quiz.why: The phone turns the shaking of her voice into a pattern and sends the pattern. If you chose the louder voice, remember that a shout reaches one street and a phone reaches another city.

quiz.p: A mobile phone has no wire. How does its signal leave the phone?
opts: A thin wire runs from every phone
As radio waves that we cannot see
Her voice flies the whole way through the air
quiz.why: Radio waves are light that our eyes cannot see, and they carry the signal to a tower. If you chose the wire, think about where the wire would be when you walk.

quiz.p: Which is the best description of the internet?
opts: One huge computer in a city
Many computers and phones joined together
A cloud in the sky
quiz.why: The internet is a network of many computers, joined by cables and radio waves. The word 'cloud' hides the real cables and buildings.

quiz.p: A phone cuts a big photo into pieces and numbers each piece. Why number them?
opts: To put them back in order at the end
To make the photo smaller
To keep strangers out
quiz.why: Pieces may travel by different roads and arrive in a mixed order. The numbers let the phone build the photo again.

quiz.p: Rani types 'Okay.' and she is happy. Her friend reads it as cross. Why?
opts: The reader cannot hear Rani's voice
The phone changed the word
Her friend was careless
quiz.why: A typed word carries no tone. The reader has to guess the feeling, and guesses often miss. Blaming the friend skips the main point.

quiz.p: Which message is least likely to be read the wrong way?
opts: A typed 'Fine.'
A voice note saying 'Fine!' warmly
A typed 'FINE'
quiz.why: A voice note carries the voice, so the reader hears the feeling. A typed word has none, and capital letters can sound angry.

quiz.p: Which of these is private information?
opts: Your favourite fruit
Your home address
Your favourite song
quiz.why: An address can lead a stranger to your door. A favourite fruit cannot lead anyone to you.

opts: Your best friend
Your parent
A kind person in a game
quiz.why: A password opens your account. A best friend today may not be one next month, and the password will still work.

quiz.p: A person in a game says, 'Keep this our secret.' What does this show?
opts: A good friend is speaking
A sign to tell a trusted adult
It is a rule of the game
quiz.why: A safe surprise, such as a birthday gift, is soon told. A secret that a stranger asks you to keep is a warning.

quiz.p: Which one is misuse of a device?
opts: Reading your uncle's messages without asking
Calling your grandmother with a parent beside you
Putting a screen lock on a phone
quiz.why: Misuse means using a device to harm, to trick, to spy or without leave. A lock and a call with a parent are safe.

quiz.p: Why does deleting a sent message not take it fully back?
opts: A copy may already be on another phone
Deleted messages come back on Tuesdays
Messages never leave the phone
quiz.why: A sent message becomes a copy on someone else's device. Deleting removes only your own copy.

quiz.p: A scary picture arrives on a screen. Which first step is right?
opts: Reply to ask who sent it
Stop, do not answer, keep it and tell an adult
Delete it at once so that nobody sees
quiz.why: The four steps keep you safe, and the adult needs to see the picture. Replying tells the sender that you are there.

quiz.p: Why should a child keep a scary message and not delete it?
opts: The adult needs to see it
Deleted messages come back to scare you
The phone breaks if a message is deleted
quiz.why: The adult can use the message to find who sent it and to help. Deleting it hides the proof.

quiz.p: A message says, 'Send this to ten people now!' What is the best first step?
opts: Send it quickly before it expires
Ask who says it and how they know
Send it to ten people to be safe
quiz.why: The two questions slow things down. A rush is a warning sign, and a few seconds of checking cost nothing.

quiz.p: A forwarded message says the school is closed tomorrow. What is the best check?
opts: Ask a teacher or the school
Count how many times it was forwarded
See if it has a nice picture
quiz.why: Many forwards do not make a thing true. The school knows. Asking the one who really knows is the best check.

quiz.p: A phone calls an ambulance and also carries a cruel message. What does that show?
opts: Phones are bad
The same tool can help or harm, depending on how it is used
Phones are good
quiz.why: A tool has no side. Its use decides what it does, and who has one decides who gets the help.

maths.problem: You send a photo to 3 cousins. Each cousin sends it on to 3 more people. Those people each send it on to 3 more. How many people have the photo after those three sends?
maths.explain: The first send reaches 3. Each of the 3 sends to 3, which is 3 × 3 = 9. Each of the 9 sends to 3, which is 9 × 3 = 27. Add 3 + 9 + 27 = 39.
maths.context: This problem uses the idea of forwarding to show how quickly copies of a message multiply.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by 3 each time grows very fast. This is why a message cannot be taken back once it is forwarded.

maths.problem: A photo is cut into 10 numbered packets. Packets 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 have arrived. Which numbers are missing, and how many?
maths.explain: List the numbers 1 to 10. Tick off those that arrived. The ones with no tick are 4 and 7. 10 - 8 = 2 missing.
maths.context: This problem uses numbered packets to find which are missing.
maths.why_maths: A phone does the same check. It looks for gaps in the numbers and asks again for the missing packets.

maths.problem: In a test, a reader gets 2 right out of 6 on the chit round, 4 on the voice round and 6 on the face round. How many more right does the face round give than the chit round?
maths.explain: 6 - 2 = 4. The scores 2, 4 and 6 also go up by 2 each time.
maths.context: This problem compares the scores of the three rounds of the message without a face test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing counts shows how much the voice and the face add.

maths.problem: A grown-up says the family should take a 20-minute near-work spell and then look far for 20 seconds. In one hour of near work, how many far-looks are there? How many seconds of far-looking in all?
maths.explain: One hour is 60 minutes. 60 ÷ 20 = 3 spells, so 3 far-looks. 3 × 20 seconds = 60 seconds.
maths.context: This problem uses the 20-20-20 habit to practise division and multiplication.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the hour into equal spells shows how often the eyes get a rest.

jokes.j: Why did the phone wear glasses?
What did the Wi-Fi say to the phone?
Why did the koel never need a phone?
jokes.a: She already had a very good call.

jokes.j: Why does an elephant never run out of data?
jokes.a: She sends her rumbles for free, and they travel for kilometres.

jokes.j: Why is a sea cable always calm?
jokes.a: Even with the whole sea sitting on top of it, it just carries on working.

jokes.j: Why did the typed 'Okay.' get into trouble?
jokes.a: Nobody could see what face it was making.

jokes.j: A 'puppy' on a game screen asked a child for her home address. What did her grandmother say?
jokes.a: 'A real puppy has never asked for an address. It only asks for biscuits.'

jokes.j: Why did the honey bee never lose her signal?
jokes.a: She sends her messages by dancing, and nobody has ever dropped a dance.

jokes.j: What did the photo say when it was cut into eight packets?
jokes.a: 'I am all in pieces, but do not worry. I will be back together by the time I reach Madurai.'

warmup.a: The shaking of your voice in the air.

warmup.q: What do mobile phones use to send a signal through the air?
warmup.a: Radio waves, a kind of light that our eyes cannot see.
Small numbered pieces of a message.

warmup.q: Name one fact about you that is private.
warmup.a: Any of: home address, school name, phone number, password, full name, a photo in uniform.

warmup.q: What are the four steps when something on a screen feels wrong?
warmup.a: Stop, do not answer, keep it, tell a trusted adult.

warmup.q: What number is Childline, the free helpline for children in India?
What number can you dial in an emergency, even on a locked phone?

quiz: A phone sends your voice as a pattern that can travel.
The phone turns the shaking of your voice into a pattern, sends it and changes it back.
A mobile phone needs a wire all the way to the other phone.
A mobile phone sends radio waves through the air to a tower, and cables carry on from there.
A typed word carries the tone of your voice.
A typed word has only the letters. The reader has to guess the feeling.
If you delete a sent message, a copy may still be on a friend's phone.
Deleting removes only your own copy.
A password is safe to share with a best friend.
A password is shared only with a parent. A best friend today may not be one next month.
Some people on a screen use a false name and a false picture.
On a screen you cannot see who is typing, so a name proves nothing.
A message that says 'Send this quickly' is a good reason to check it first.
Hurry is a warning sign. Taking a moment to check costs nothing.
You should tell a trusted adult when something online scares you.
Telling brings help, and it is never your fault.
A real bank asks you to read out your one-time password.
A real bank never asks for it. Anyone who asks is trying to steal.
A phone is a tool, so what it does depends on how people use it.
A phone can call help or carry cruelty. The choice is made by the person.
odd: A phone, a tablet and a laptop are devices. A radio wave is what they use to send signals.
A password, an address and a school name could lead a stranger to you. A favourite fruit cannot.
Stop, keep it and tell an adult are the safe steps. Replying tells the sender that you are there.
A tower, a cable and glass fibre are parts of how messages travel. A stranger is a person.
An elephant, a bee and an ant send messages with their own bodies. A cup phone is a tool that people make.

spotted.text: Look up on a roof or a hill for a tall mobile tower. Notice the flat boxes on top that point in different directions. Each one talks to phones in its own part of the neighbourhood.
spotted.art: A tall tower on a roof with three flat boxes pointing in different directions, with coconut palms below.

spotted.text: Walk into a lift or a basement with a grown-up and watch the signal bars on their phone. Notice that the bars shrink, because thick concrete and metal stop radio waves.
spotted.art: A grown-up's phone in a lift with the signal bars dropping from four to one.

spotted.text: When a grown-up's video call freezes and a circle turns, notice that the call has stopped. Packets are late, and the phone is waiting for them to arrive.
spotted.art: A phone screen showing a face frozen in mid-smile and a small circle turning.

spotted.text: Look at an ATM or a shop's card machine. Notice how the person covers the number pad with a hand when they type their secret number. Covering the secret is a habit that you can copy for any password.
spotted.art: A person's hand hiding a number pad while a second hand types.

spotted.text: Look for the number 1098 on school walls, in railway stations and on notice boards. Notice that the number is there for any child who needs help.
spotted.art: A school notice board with the number 1098 painted in bright colours.

spotted.text: Listen to a koel in a mango tree in March, and to another koel that answers from far away. Notice that a call carries a long way without a phone.
spotted.art: A male koel with his beak open on a mango branch, and a second koel faint in the distance.

spotted.text: After a long time drawing or reading, notice how your eyes feel. Then look at a far hill or tower and notice the feeling change.
spotted.art: A child looking up from a book through a window at a far hill.

applications: Fishing families on the Kerala coast use mobile phones to hear weather warnings and to call the markets from their boats, to find where their catch will sell. This is one use of the same phone that can carry a cruel message.
Dialling 112 on any phone reaches the police, an ambulance or the fire service. This works even on a locked phone, so a child can call for help from a parent's phone.
A video call lets a child in Bengaluru see a grandparent in Shillong, and a child who cannot hear can talk with friends in sign language. A phone lets people stay close across great distances.
Phones and tablets can read text aloud for people who cannot see well. The same radio waves and packets carry the voice to the person who needs it.
Shops and vegetable sellers across India take payment by scanning a code with a phone. The payment is a message in packets, and the secret number that confirms it must never be shared.
A school can send a notice to every family at once. Because anyone can copy a message, a family should check that a notice really comes from the school before passing it on.

Phone companies and repair markets, such as Ritchie Street in Chennai, give old phones a second life by mending them. A phone that is mended and used for years means fewer metals are dug from the ground.
